name: PSAT/NMSQT
blurb: Reading and Writing at the hard-module level, math with no careless misses, and timed modules

units.title: The plan and test day
units.blurb: The Selection Index arithmetic with your own numbers, why Reading and Writing is where the points are, how the adaptive modules work, and the pacing and test-day routine.
keys: Selection Index = 2 × (RW ÷ 10) + (Math ÷ 10); each PSAT section tops out at 760, so the maximum is 228.
Your numbers: 730 and 790 give about 2 × 73 + 76 = 222; each 10 RW points is 2 index points; 760 RW makes 228.
Math is at the cap already; its job is zero careless misses. Reading and Writing counts double and is where the points are.
Cutoffs vary by state and year: recently, from around the Commended level (a little above 205) in the least competitive states to the low-to-mid 220s in the most competitive.
Module 1 decides whether module 2 is the harder version, and only the harder version reaches the top scores.
Pacing: about 71 seconds per Reading and Writing question and about 95 per math question; flag, guess and return.
No penalty for wrong answers: never leave a blank.

topics.t: The Selection Index and the strategy

units.title: Craft and structure
units.blurb: Words in context with the rare sense of a common word, purpose questions decided by the verb, and cross-text questions decided by exactly what Text 2 accepts and disputes.
keys: Predict a word from the context clue before reading the choices; the first dictionary meaning is the standing trap.
Check, command, qualify, grave, appreciate, sanction, arrest, entertain, betray and temper all have a second sense the hard module loves.
In a precision blank, match both the charge (frugal vs stingy) and the strength (consistent with vs prove) the context allows.
In a purpose or structure question, judge the verb first: describe, explain, argue, challenge and qualify are different jobs.
A sentence that keeps a finding but narrows it qualifies; only a sentence that says the finding is wrong refutes.
In cross-text questions, state Text 1's specific claim, then find Text 2's stance on that claim alone.
The hard cross-text answer is usually partial: Text 2 accepts the finding and disputes the explanation or the scope.

units.title: Information and ideas
units.blurb: Main ideas that survive the turn, evidence that matches the exact claim, data choices that are true in every word and serve the claim, and inferences that must be true rather than could be.
keys: The main idea is the claim every sentence serves; when the text turns ("In fact," "Yet," "Until"), look after the turn.
"According to the text" means only the text: a true outside fact is a wrong answer.
A supporting finding matches the claim's subject, variable, direction and scope, and isolates the claimed cause from its rivals.
"Consistent with" is not "supports": a finding every rival explanation predicts supports none of them.
In quantitative evidence, every number and every comparison word in the choice must be true of the table, and the choice must speak to the specific claim.
A proportion claim needs shares, a benefit claim needs a comparison with the control, and an "all" claim falls to one counterexample.
An inference must be true given the text; "could be" and "goes too far" are the two traps, and with conditionals only the contrapositive is valid.

units.title: Standard English conventions
units.blurb: The boundary and form rules that decide the hard-module conventions questions, each tested on a fresh sentence. Every card turns on one question: what is the clause structure, and what does the grammar, not the ear, require?
keys: Find the independent clauses first: a subject plus a finite verb with no subordinating word; that count decides every boundary question.

Two independent clauses join only with a period, a semicolon, a colon (or a dash doing a colon's job), or a comma plus for, and, nor, but, or, yet or so; "however," "then" and "for example" cannot join them.
Whatever stands before a colon (or a single dash doing a colon's job) must be a complete sentence.
Paired punctuation around a nonessential element must match (comma–comma or dash–dash), and nothing separates a subject from its verb or a verb from its object.
A title before a name ("the chemist Rosalind Franklin") and a that-clause are restrictive and take no commas.
Strike every phrase and clause between subject and verb, and look after the verb in inverted sentences, before choosing a verb form; collective nouns are singular.
Let the time cue choose the tense: "since" wants the present perfect, "by the time" plus a past event the past perfect.
An introductory modifier describes the noun right after the comma; a possessive (Cameron's portraits) cannot be that noun.

units.title: Expression of ideas
units.blurb: Transitions as named logical relations and rhetorical synthesis as goal-matching. The hard versions hide the relation two sentences back, or put the right facts under the wrong goal.
keys: Name the relation between the sentences in your own words before looking at the choices.
After a concession ("admittedly," "only 24 patients"), ask whether the next sentence holds DESPITE it (nevertheless) or FOLLOWS from it (accordingly).
An example is a case of the specific claim just made; a separate point about the same subject is addition.
Similarly and likewise mark a parallel case (a new subject doing the same thing); moreover adds another point about the same subject.
By contrast compares two subjects; nevertheless pushes against one claim; instead replaces something ruled out; meanwhile means at the same time.
In rhetorical synthesis, every choice is accurate to the notes; only the goal separates them.
Require every part of the goal: a difference names both things; "unfamiliar" needs a description; aim and method need both; a finding plus a limitation needs both.

units.title: Math: the last few points
units.blurb: The careless-miss catalogue for a 790 scorer and the Desmos moves that save time, each on a fresh problem. At the PSAT's 760 cap, the job is to give nothing away.
keys: Before answering, reread what the question asks for: the value of an expression, the y-coordinate, hours not minutes, the maximum value not where it occurs.
Check every root of a squared or rational equation in the original; squaring and clearing denominators create extraneous solutions.
"Must be true" needs a counterexample test on every other choice; "could be" is not enough.
Successive percent changes multiply, and each percent is taken of its own base: the word after "of" or "than" names it.
With "at most" round down; with "greater than" the boundary value fails; read a table's given condition as the denominator.
A line of best fit gives predicted values; a data point is an actual value; a sample speaks only for the population it was drawn from.
Desmos: y₁ ~ for regression, sliders to explore but the discriminant to confirm, click intersections and vertices, and enter decimals that fill every space.
SPR: no mixed numbers, no symbols, 5 characters for a positive answer and 6 for a negative one; a non-terminating decimal must fill them.

cards.q: How does National Merit compute the Selection Index from PSAT/NMSQT scores, and what is its range?
cards.a: Selection Index = 2 × (Reading and Writing ÷ 10) + (Math ÷ 10), the same as (2 × RW + Math) ÷ 10. Each section is scored 160 to 760 on the PSAT/NMSQT, so the index runs from 48 to 228. Reading and Writing counts twice.
cards.n: Adding the two section scores and dividing by 10 (as if the total score mattered); the index weights Reading and Writing double.

cards.q: On the September SAT you scored 730 Reading and Writing and 790 Math. If you perform at the same level on the PSAT/NMSQT, what Selection Index does that give?
cards.a: About 222. The PSAT/NMSQT caps each section at 760, so Math counts as 76, not 79; Reading and Writing counts 73, doubled. 2 × 73 + 76 = 146 + 76 = 222.
cards.n: Using 79 for math (2 × 73 + 79 = 225); the PSAT's 760 ceiling means math can add at most 76.

cards.q: With Math at 760, what Reading and Writing score gives a Selection Index of 228? Of 226? Of 224?
cards.a: 760, 750 and 740. With Math contributing 76, the index is 2 × (RW ÷ 10) + 76: 2 × 76 + 76 = 228, 2 × 75 + 76 = 226, 2 × 74 + 76 = 224. Every 10 Reading and Writing points is 2 index points, so each step from 730 adds 2.
cards.n: Thinking the index moves 1 per 10 points in both sections; RW moves it by 2.

cards.q: Why is Reading and Writing, not Math, where your remaining index points are?
cards.a: Math is already at the PSAT's ceiling: 790 skill maps to the 760 cap, so the most math can do is hold 76. Reading and Writing counts double and has room: 730 → 760 is +6 on the index (222 → 228). Because every RW point counts double, one Reading and Writing question is worth more to the index than one math question, very roughly one and a half to two times as much (RW has more questions, so each moves fewer scaled points). So prep time goes to the hardest Reading and Writing question types, and math prep is about not giving points away.
cards.h: → math's job + RW's room + where prep time goes
cards.n: Spending prep time where you are already strong feels productive; it cannot raise an index that math has already maxed.

cards.q: A 730 Reading and Writing score means a handful of misses across the two modules. Which question types are they almost always, at your level?
cards.a: The hardest ones: an inference where the tempting choice could be true but need not be; a cross-text question where Text 2 partly agrees; words in context with a rare sense of a common word ("check," "qualify," "sanction"); a textual or quantitative evidence question whose tempting choice is true but does not support the specific claim; and a boundaries question that turns on whether something is an independent clause. The craft, info, conventions and expression decks drill exactly these.
cards.n: Reviewing every question type evenly; at 730, the easy and medium questions are already right, and only the hard traps are costing points.

cards.q: What are the recent National Merit cutoffs, and how should you think about them?
cards.a: Cutoffs vary by state and by year, so no single number is safe to plan around. In recent years the Commended level has sat a little above 205, and state Semifinalist cutoffs have ranged from around that level in the least competitive states to the low-to-mid 220s in the most competitive ones. The Commended cutoff is national; Semifinalist cutoffs are set state by state after the test. A 222 clears the Commended level and the Semifinalist cutoff in most states, but may fall short in the most competitive ones; 228 is the ceiling.
cards.n: Treating last year's cutoff for your state as a fixed target; it moves year to year, so aim as high as the ceiling allows.

cards.q: What is the structure of the digital PSAT/NMSQT: sections, modules, questions and time?
cards.a: Reading and Writing first: two modules of 27 questions, 32 minutes each. Then a 10-minute break. Then Math: two modules of 22 questions, 35 minutes each, with Desmos built in and a reference sheet. Every Reading and Writing question has its own short passage; about a quarter of math questions are student-produced responses.
cards.h: → two sections × two modules, counts and minutes
cards.n: Assuming you can return to module 1 later; once a module's time ends, its questions are closed.

cards.q: How does the adaptive design work, and why does a strong first module matter?
cards.a: Each section is adaptive by module. Module 1 has a broad mix of easy, medium and hard questions. Your performance on it decides whether module 2 is the harder or the easier version. Only the harder module 2 makes the top of the scale reachable, and scoring takes each question's difficulty into account. So module 1 is not a warm-up: careless misses there can cap the whole section. It also means a module 2 that feels hard is good news.
cards.h: → how routing works + what it means for module 1
cards.n: Rushing module 1 because it feels easy; accuracy there decides which scores are still possible.

cards.q: Can you work out exactly how many misses a 760 allows?
cards.a: No. Scores come from a statistical model that weights questions by difficulty, each module includes a few unscored pretest questions you cannot identify, and the scale differs from form to form. At the very top, what one Reading and Writing miss costs varies from form to form, often 10 points or more. Plan for zero misses on the questions you can control and treat every question as if it counts.
cards.n: Using a raw-score chart from another test to decide that a miss or two is "free"; the cost varies by form.

cards.q: Math: 790 on the SAT is above the PSAT's 760 cap. Does that mean math needs no preparation?
cards.a: No. The cap gives some cushion, but a careless miss or two in the hard math module can pull the score under 760 on some forms, and each 10 math points is 1 index point. Math prep is maintenance: a timed module or two, the careless-miss checklist (what is asked, units, extraneous roots, "must be true," percent bases, strict inequalities, SPR entry rules), and the Desmos moves.
cards.h: → no + what math prep is for
cards.n: Treating 790 as a guarantee; a guarantee needs zero careless misses, which is a habit, not a score.

cards.q: A week of prep time is left. How should you divide it between Reading and Writing and Math?
cards.a: Mostly Reading and Writing: most of the time on the hard RW types (inferences, cross-text, rare-sense words in context, evidence that must match the claim, boundaries), practiced on timed sets and reviewed by why the trap tempted you. A smaller share on math, to keep speed and the checklist sharp. One full timed practice test early in the week, reviewed miss by miss. No new content in the last two days.
cards.h: → the split + what fills each part
cards.n: An even split feels balanced, but RW points are worth double and math is already at the cap.

cards.q: How many seconds per question do you have on average in a Reading and Writing module? In a math module?
cards.a: Reading and Writing: 32 minutes × 60 ÷ 27 questions ≈ 71 seconds per question. Math: 35 × 60 ÷ 22 ≈ 95 seconds per question.
cards.n: Treating 71 seconds as a limit for every question; conventions questions take less, and the saved time funds the hard inferences and cross-text questions.

cards.q: In a Reading and Writing module, where should you be when 16 of the 32 minutes are gone, and why is being slightly behind even pace acceptable?
cards.a: Around question 12 or 13. Even pace (71 seconds each) would put you at about question 13 or 14, but the module runs in a fixed order: the reading-heavy craft and information questions come first, and the conventions and transition questions later go much faster. If you are well short of question 11 at halfway, speed up on the next easy-looking question and use flag-and-return.
cards.h: → a checkpoint + why the order allows it
cards.n: Panicking at being slightly behind halfway, then rushing a hard inference; the back half of a module is faster.

cards.q: What is the flag-and-return rule for a question that is eating time?
cards.a: In Reading and Writing, if you are about 90 seconds in and still torn between two choices (longer in math), pick your best current guess, mark it for review in Bluebook, and move on. At the end of the module, use the navigator to return to marked questions with fresh eyes. You can move freely within a module until its time runs out, but not back into a finished module.
cards.h: → the trigger + the three steps + the limit
cards.n: Leaving a flagged question blank "for now"; always enter a guess first, in case time runs out.

cards.q: Is there a penalty for a wrong answer on the PSAT/NMSQT, and what follows from that?
cards.a: No: wrong answers and blanks both earn nothing. So answer every question. Eliminate what you can, choose between the survivors, and before the module's time ends, check the navigator for any unanswered question and fill it in. Never leave a blank.
cards.n: Leaving a question blank because a guess "might be wrong"; a blank is always wrong.

cards.q: You finish a math module with ten minutes left. What is the best use of that time?
cards.a: First return to marked questions. Then re-read the last line of each harder question, checking against the careless-miss list: did you answer what was asked (value of an expression, y-coordinate, hours not minutes)? Did you check roots in the original equation? Is every SPR entry in an accepted form? Use Desmos to verify answers you found by hand (graph both sides, check an intersection).
cards.n: Resting, or re-solving easy questions in full; the misses at your level come from misreading what was asked, so check that first.

cards.q: Which Bluebook tools should you know well before test day?
cards.a: The countdown timer (you can hide it; Bluebook warns you when about five minutes remain), Mark for Review and the question navigator, the option eliminator for crossing out choices, the annotation tool in Reading and Writing, and in Math the built-in Desmos graphing calculator and the reference sheet. Take the official practice test in Bluebook so none of these is new on the day.
cards.n: Learning Desmos's regression or slider syntax during the test; practice the moves beforehand.

cards.q: What should the week before the test look like?
cards.a: Early in the week: one full, timed practice PSAT in Bluebook, under test conditions, then a careful review of every miss by type. Midweek: short timed sets on your weakest Reading and Writing types, plus a math module. Update Bluebook and complete whatever exam setup your school asks for. Shift your sleep so you are waking at test-day time. Last two days: light review of high-yield cards only, no new material and no full-length test.
cards.h: → early week, midweek, last two days
cards.n: Cramming a full practice test the night before; fatigue costs more than one more test teaches.

cards.q: What should you do the morning of the test and during the break?
cards.a: Morning: normal sleep and a real breakfast; bring your charged device and charger, pencils for scratch paper, any approved calculator you use, a snack and water for the break, and whatever your school's instructions require. Arrive early. A few easy warm-up questions in the morning are fine; hard new material is not. Break: eat, drink, move, and do not discuss or replay the Reading and Writing questions. The math section is a fresh start.
cards.n: Spending the break reliving a hard Reading and Writing question; it cannot change, and it costs focus for math.

cards.q: Module 2 of Reading and Writing feels noticeably harder than module 1. What does that likely mean, and how should you respond?
cards.a: It likely means module 1 went well and you were routed to the harder module, which is the one that makes the top scores reachable. Keep the same process: read each passage for its claim, name the relation before looking at choices, flag and return when a question stalls. Do not speed up to "get through" the hard ones; at your level, they are the questions that decide the score.
cards.h: → what it means + keep the process
cards.n: Reading difficulty as failure and rushing; the harder module is the sign you want.

cards.q: Words in Context on the hard module usually uses a common word in a less common sense ("check," "command," "qualify," "grave," "appreciate"). What is the move, and what is the trap?
cards.a: Cover the choices and predict a word of your own from the sentence's clue (what the subject can physically do, what an "although" contrasts). Then choose the option closest to your prediction. The trap is the word's first dictionary meaning: it is almost always among the choices, and it sounds right on its own. Substitute each finalist into the sentence; the right one keeps the sentence's logic, not just its grammar.
cards.h: → the move in two steps + the trap
cards.n: Reading the choices first lets the familiar meaning anchor you before you have used the context.

cards.q:
"Planting dense hedgerows along the field edges helped check the spread of the fungus, whose spores travel on the wind."
As used in the text, what does the word "check" most nearly mean?
(A) inspect
(B) mark
(C) verify
(D) restrain
cards.a: (D). The hedgerows block wind-borne spores, so they hold back the spread: "check" in the sense of "keep in check." (A) and (C) are the everyday senses (examine, confirm), but hedgerows cannot inspect or verify anything. (B) is the sense of a check mark.
cards.n: "Inspect" is the meaning you use every day, and "check the spread" can sound like monitoring it; ask what a hedgerow can physically do.

cards.q:
"Perched on a ridge above the harbor, the old fortress commands a view of every ship entering the bay."
As used in the text, what does the word "commands" most nearly mean?
(A) orders
(B) overlooks
(C) demands
(D) earns
cards.a: (B). From a high ridge, the fortress looks down on the bay: to command a view is to overlook it from a dominant position. (A) is giving orders. (C) and (D) are the senses in "commands respect" and "commands a high price," which do not fit a view.
cards.n: "Earns" is tempting because "command respect" is a familiar phrase; a view is not something a building earns.

cards.q:
"Although the author's early novels sold poorly, first editions of them now command prices of several thousand dollars at auction."
As used in the text, what does the word "command" most nearly mean?
(A) bring in
(B) order
(C) control
(D) request
cards.a: (A). The first editions sell for, or fetch, several thousand dollars: "command a price" means to bring in that price. (B) and (C) are the military and managerial senses. (D) is too weak and has the wrong agent: books cannot request anything, and the prices are actually paid.
cards.n: "Control" sounds like the core meaning of command; prices are paid, not controlled.

cards.q:
"Although the reviewer admired the novel's ambitious structure, she qualified her praise, noting that several of the late chapters felt rushed."
As used in the text, what does the word "qualified" most nearly mean?
(A) intensified
(B) earned
(C) certified
(D) limited
cards.a: (D). She admired the structure but added a reservation (the rushed chapters), so she restricted her praise. To qualify a statement is to limit it. (C) is the sense of qualifying for a job or a race. (B) fails because praise is not earned by the one giving it. (A) is the opposite.
cards.n: "Certified" is the everyday sense (qualified for the job); in claims and praise, qualify means to narrow.

cards.q:
"Engineers warned that the widening cracks in the dam's spillway posed a grave risk to the towns downstream."
As used in the text, what does the word "grave" most nearly mean?
(A) serious
(B) solemn
(C) dignified
(D) buried
cards.a: (A). A risk from a cracking dam is serious, or dangerous. (B) and (C) describe a person's manner ("a grave expression"), which is the wrong kind of thing to describe a risk. (D) confuses the adjective with the noun.
cards.n: "Solemn" is a real meaning of grave, which is why it tempts; match the sense to the noun it modifies.

cards.q:
"Only after the drought did the town's residents fully appreciate how heavily their farms depended on the aquifer beneath them."
As used in the text, what does the word "appreciate" most nearly mean?
(A) be grateful for
(B) increase in value
(C) recognize
(D) enjoy
cards.a: (C). The drought made them grasp, or fully understand, a fact they had overlooked: appreciate "how heavily..." means recognize it. (A) does not fit an object like "how heavily their farms depended." (B) is the financial sense. (D) contradicts the drought context.
cards.n: "Be grateful for" is the everyday sense and fits many sentences; it does not fit a "how" clause about dependence.

cards.q:
"Although the city council never formally sanctioned the weekend street market, it made no effort to shut the market down."
As used in the text, what does the word "sanctioned" most nearly mean?
(A) penalized
(B) publicized
(C) inspected
(D) authorized
cards.a: (D). "Although" sets up a contrast: the council never approved the market, yet it let the market run. (A) is the word's opposite sense, and it would erase the contrast: never penalizing a market and not shutting it down agree with each other, so "although" would make no sense. (C) and (B) do not create the contrast either.
cards.n: "Sanction" means both approve and penalize; the logic word (although) decides which one, and strong students who know only the penalty sense miss it.

cards.q:
"The new therapy could not reverse the damage to patients' nerves, but it did arrest the disease's progress for as long as five years."
As used in the text, what does the word "arrest" most nearly mean?
(A) halt
(B) seize
(C) capture
(D) attract
cards.a: (A). The contrast is between reversing the damage (not possible) and stopping further progress (possible), so arrest means halt. (B) and (C) are the police sense. (D) is the sense of "an arresting image," one that grabs attention.
cards.n: "Arresting" as striking is the sophisticated sense students reach for on a hard module; the contrast with "reverse" asks for "stop."

cards.q:
"The board refused even to entertain the proposal, rejecting it before the architects had a chance to present their drawings."
As used in the text, what does the word "entertain" most nearly mean?
(A) consider
(B) host
(C) amuse
(D) perform
cards.a: (A). Rejecting a proposal before it is presented means refusing to consider it at all: to entertain an idea is to give it consideration. (C) and (D) are the performance senses and (B) the hospitality sense; none fits a proposal.
cards.h: → letter + what the board refused to do
cards.n: "Host" can feel right because the architects came to the meeting; the object of "entertain" is the proposal, not the architects.

cards.q:
"Though the diplomat's words were carefully measured, a slight tremor in her voice betrayed her anxiety."
As used in the text, what does the word "betrayed" most nearly mean?
(A) deceived
(B) abandoned
(C) revealed
(D) exaggerated
cards.a: (C). Her words hid her feelings, but the tremor showed them without her meaning to: betray in the sense of reveal unintentionally. (A) and (B) are the disloyalty senses, which need a person as the victim. (D) adds a meaning the text does not support.
cards.n: Betrayal as treachery is the dominant sense; a voice cannot be disloyal to an emotion.

cards.q:
"The evidence linking the two carved boxes to the same workshop is ______: both bear a spiral motif, but so do hundreds of other objects from the period."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) conclusive
(B) tenuous
(C) fabricated
(D) irrelevant
cards.a: (B). The shared motif is some evidence, but weak, since hundreds of other objects share it: tenuous (thin, slight) is exact. (A) is the opposite. (D) overshoots, because a shared motif is relevant, just not strong. (C) accuses someone of inventing evidence, which nothing in the text suggests.
cards.h: → letter + how strong the evidence is
cards.n: "Irrelevant" feels right because the evidence fails; weak evidence is still relevant, and the precise word names its weakness.

cards.q:
"Colleagues remembered the physicist as ______ rather than stingy: she reused old envelopes for her calculations yet gave generously to her students' travel fund."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) miserly
(B) impoverished
(C) wasteful
(D) frugal
cards.a: (D). The text separates careful thrift (reusing envelopes) from stinginess (she gave generously), so the word must mean "careful with resources" with a positive charge: frugal. (A) is a synonym of the stingy that "rather than" rules out. (C) is the opposite of reusing envelopes. (B) says she was poor, which the text never suggests.
cards.n: Miserly and frugal share a denotation (saving); "rather than stingy" makes the negative one wrong.

cards.q:
"The results ______ the hypothesis that the moths navigate by the Moon, but the authors caution that a single season of data cannot rule out other cues, such as the glow of distant cities."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
(A) are consistent with
(B) prove
(C) refute
(D) ignore
cards.a: (A). The results fit the hypothesis, but the authors say other explanations remain open, so the precise phrase is "are consistent with." (B) is too strong: if other cues cannot be ruled out, the hypothesis is not proved. (C) contradicts the "but" (the caution only makes sense if the results favor the hypothesis). (D) makes no sense for results.
cards.h: → letter + how much the caution allows
cards.n: "Prove" feels natural in a science sentence; the caution clause caps how strong the verb can be.

cards.q:
"The committee found the proposal wanting: its budget left out maintenance costs entirely."
As used in the text, what does the word "wanting" most nearly mean?
(A) desirable
(B) eager
(C) deficient
(D) ambitious
cards.a: (C). The colon's explanation names a gap (maintenance costs left out), so the proposal fell short: wanting in the sense of lacking. (A) and (B) are the desire senses. (D) fits the topic, but the colon points to a flaw, not a scale.
cards.n: "Desirable" comes from reading "wanting" as "something we want"; the explanation after the colon is a defect.

cards.q:
"The crowd's relief at the rescue was tempered by the news that two climbers were still missing."
As used in the text, what does the word "tempered" most nearly mean?
(A) hardened
(B) delayed
(C) provoked
(D) moderated
cards.a: (D). The bad news reduced the relief without erasing it, so tempered means moderated, or softened. (A) comes from tempered steel or glass, a craft sense that does not fit a feeling. (C) confuses temper with a bad temper. (B) is not a meaning of the word.
cards.h: → letter + what the news did to the relief
cards.n: "Hardened" is the technical sense strong students know from science; relief is not a metal.

cards.q:
"The calm surface of the lake belies the strong currents that run beneath it."
As used in the text, what does the word "belies" most nearly mean?
(A) reveals
(B) disguises
(C) produces
(D) confirms
cards.a: (B). A calm surface gives a false impression of what lies below: to belie is to misrepresent or disguise. (A) and (D) are near-opposites, the usual trap with this word. (C) invents a causal link the sentence does not make.
cards.n: "Belie" is often misread as "betray" or "reveal"; the contrast between calm and strong requires "hide."

cards.q: In a Text Structure and Purpose question, each choice is a verb plus an object ("to argue that...," "to describe...," "to challenge..."). How do you eliminate efficiently, and which verbs are the usual traps?
cards.a: Judge the verb first. Ask what the author is DOING: describing or reporting (neutral), explaining how or why, arguing for a position, challenging or refuting a claim, qualifying (limiting) one. Cross out every choice whose verb overstates or misstates the author's stance, then check the object of the survivors against the whole text, not one sentence. The usual traps: "argue" or "advocate" for a text that only describes; "refute" for a text that only qualifies; "criticize" for a text that reports a limitation.
cards.h: → verb first, then object + the three trap verbs
cards.n: A choice whose object repeats the passage's words exactly is tempting, but a wrong verb kills it however familiar its object sounds.

cards.q:
"In the Andes, wild vicuñas are sheared only once every two or three years, in roundups called chaccus that date back to the Inca Empire. Villagers form a long human chain to guide the animals into temporary corrals, shear them, and then release them unharmed to the high grasslands."
Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
(A) To argue that the chaccu should be adopted in other parts of the world
(B) To describe a traditional method of collecting wool from wild animals
(C) To challenge the idea that vicuñas are difficult to catch
(D) To compare Inca methods of shearing with modern methods
cards.a: (B). The text reports what a chaccu is and how it works, with no evaluation: its verb is "describe." (A) needs the author to advocate something. (C) needs a claim the text pushes against, and there is none. (D) needs a second, modern method, which the text never mentions.
cards.n: A text that sounds admiring ("unharmed") tempts "argue"; admiration without a recommendation is still description.

cards.q:
"For centuries, admirers of ancient Greek sculpture assumed that the statues had been meant to be seen as bare white marble. Analyses of faint pigment traces, some visible only under ultraviolet light, have shown that many of the statues were originally painted in bright colors."
Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
(A) It presents a long-held assumption and then describes evidence that contradicts it.
(B) It describes a debate among scholars and then argues that neither side has enough evidence.
(C) It explains why admirers valued bare marble and then questions whether that value was justified.
(D) It presents a technique for detecting pigments and then describes the technique's limitations.
cards.a: (A). Sentence 1 states the old assumption (bare white marble); sentence 2 reports evidence that many statues were painted. (B) invents a debate and a verdict. (C) invents an explanation of why people valued marble. (D) takes the ultraviolet detail for the text's subject and invents limitations.
cards.n: (D) picks up a vivid detail (ultraviolet light) and builds a structure around it; the structure question is about the whole text.

cards.q:
"Ecologist Tamsin Reyes expected that beavers reintroduced to a Nevada valley would raise the water table near their dams. What she did not expect was their effect on wildfire: during a 2021 fire, the valley's dammed stretches stayed green while the surrounding land burned. Reyes now argues that beaver restoration should be part of the region's fire-management plans."
Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
(A) It explains the method Reyes used to measure the water table.
(B) It describes a result that confirms the expectation stated in the first sentence.
(C) It offers a criticism of the reintroduction described in the first sentence.
(D) It presents an unexpected observation that leads to the argument in the third sentence.
cards.a: (D). "What she did not expect" marks the observation as a surprise, and the third sentence's argument ("Reyes now argues") grows from it. (B) contradicts "did not expect." (C) fails because the observation favors the beavers. (A) fails because no method is described.
cards.n: (B) is tempting because the fire effect is good news, like the expected one; the text says outright it was NOT the expected result.

cards.q:
"Marine biologist Oren Talbot found that clownfish raised in more acidic water were slower to recognize predators by smell. The effect was large in fish raised at the acidity projected for the year 2100. It was small, however, at the acidity of today's oceans, and Talbot cautions against concluding that reef fish are already impaired."
Which choice best describes the function of the third sentence in the overall structure of the text?
(A) It refutes the finding presented in the first sentence.
(B) It limits the scope of the finding presented in the first two sentences.
(C) It offers an example that illustrates the finding in the second sentence.
(D) It describes a method used to test the finding in the first sentence.
cards.a: (B). The third sentence keeps the finding but narrows it: the effect is small at present-day acidity, so it should not be applied to reef fish today. (A) is too strong; nothing says the finding is wrong. (C) fails because a small effect is not an example of a large one. (D) fails because no method is described.
cards.n: "However" and "cautions" sound like a rebuttal; a sentence that keeps the finding and limits its reach qualifies it, not refutes it.

cards.q:
"Some historians argue that the printing press spread literacy across Europe within a few decades of 1450. This view has merit: the number of books in circulation rose sharply after Gutenberg. But books do not teach people to read, and in many regions literacy rose substantially only with the spread of schooling in later centuries."
Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
(A) It states the main claim that the rest of the text supports.
(B) It concedes that the historians' view has some support before the text challenges that view.
(C) It introduces a second group of historians who disagree with the first.
(D) It explains how Gutenberg's press worked.
cards.a: (B). "This view has merit" grants the historians a point (more books), and the "But" sentence then challenges their conclusion. (A) is wrong because the text's main claim comes in the third sentence, and it pushes against the view. (C) invents a second group. (D) fails because the sentence says nothing about how the press worked.
cards.n: (A) is tempting because the sentence sounds approving; a concession is a step the author gives up before turning.

cards.q:
"Many coastal cities protect their shorelines with concrete seawalls. But seawalls reflect wave energy back toward the sea, scouring away the beach in front of them. Some cities have instead built 'living shorelines' of marsh grass and oyster reef, which absorb wave energy. These take years to become established, however, and offer little protection in the meantime."
Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
(A) It presents a problem, proposes a solution, and shows that the solution has no drawbacks.
(B) It argues that seawalls should be replaced everywhere by living shorelines.
(C) It compares the costs of two shoreline methods and concludes that one is cheaper.
(D) It describes a conventional approach and a problem with it, then presents an alternative and a drawback of that alternative.
cards.a: (D). The text moves from seawalls, to their problem (scouring), to living shorelines, to their limitation (years to establish). (B) ignores the final drawback and the text's neutral stance. (C) invents costs. (A) contradicts the last sentence.
cards.n: (B) matches the middle of the text; the last sentence's "however" keeps the text from advocating.

cards.q:
"The following text is from Jane Austen's 1813 novel Pride and Prejudice.
It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife. However little known the feelings or views of such a man may be on his first entering a neighbourhood, this truth is so well fixed in the minds of the surrounding families, that he is considered as the rightful property of some one or other of their daughters."
Which choice best describes the function of the second sentence in the overall structure of the text?
(A) It describes the arrival of a particular wealthy man in the neighborhood.
(B) It offers evidence that wealthy single men do in fact seek wives.
(C) It reveals that the "truth" stated in the first sentence is really the belief of local families, whatever the man himself may want.
(D) It criticizes the man for ignoring the families' wishes.
cards.a: (C). The second sentence shows that the "universal" truth lives "in the minds of the surrounding families," while the man's own "feelings or views" are "little known," so the first sentence is ironic. (B) takes the first sentence at face value. (A) is wrong because the text speaks of "such a man" in general. (D) invents a criticism of the man.
cards.n: (B) reads the famous first sentence literally; the second sentence exists to undercut it.

cards.q:
"The following text is from William Shakespeare's Sonnet 130. The poem begins:
My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun;
Coral is far more red than her lips' red;
It continues through ten more lines of unflattering comparisons and ends:
And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare
As any she belied with false compare."
Which choice best describes the function of the final two lines in the overall structure of the poem?
(A) They shift the poem's focus from the beloved to the speaker's own faults.
(B) They confirm that the speaker finds his beloved unattractive.
(C) They reverse the apparent criticism, suggesting that the speaker's love needs no false comparisons to be valued.
(D) They introduce a rival whose beauty the speaker prefers.
cards.a: (C). "And yet" turns the poem: the speaker says his beloved is as "rare" (precious) as any woman misrepresented ("belied") by flattering comparisons. The plain descriptions were a rejection of false praise, not of her. (B) ignores the turn. (A) and (D) invent a new subject and a rival.
cards.n: The twelve lines of put-downs set up (B); the couplet exists to overturn them, which is the sonnet's structure.

cards.q:
"Mrs. Aldine set the table for four, though only she and her son would eat. She had done this every evening since the spring, straightening the two extra forks as if someone might inspect them. Her son had stopped remarking on it weeks ago."
Which choice best describes the function of the detail about the extra forks?
(A) It suggests that Mrs. Aldine keeps up a routine connected to people who are no longer at the table.
(B) It shows that Mrs. Aldine expects guests that evening.
(C) It indicates that Mrs. Aldine is careless about household tasks.
(D) It reveals that her son disapproves of the routine.
cards.a: (A). Setting places for two people who never come, every evening since spring and with care, points to a habit tied to people who are absent. (B) is contradicted by "every evening since the spring" (a routine, not a plan for tonight). (C) is the opposite of straightening forks. (D) overreads the son's silence.
cards.n: (D) seizes the last sentence; "stopped remarking" shows resignation or habit, not stated disapproval, and the question asks about the forks.

cards.q:
"Many guidebooks repeat the claim that the Great Wall of China can be seen from the Moon with the naked eye. Astronauts who have looked report otherwise. Although the wall is thousands of kilometers long, it is mostly less than 10 meters wide and close in color to the land around it; even from low Earth orbit it is very difficult to pick out."
Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
(A) To challenge a popular claim by citing firsthand reports and physical features of the wall
(B) To describe how the Great Wall of China was built
(C) To argue that astronauts' observations are unreliable
(D) To explain why the wall was built in narrow sections
cards.a: (A). The text names a popular claim and then refutes it with astronauts' reports and the wall's width and color. (B) and (D) are about construction, which the text never discusses. (C) reverses the text, which relies on astronauts' reports.
cards.n: (D) grabs "less than 10 meters wide" and turns a piece of evidence into the purpose; the width serves the challenge.

cards.q: Cross-text questions ("Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to...?") are where strong readers lose points. What are the two moves and the three traps?
cards.a: Moves: (1) State Text 1's specific claim in a phrase. (2) Find Text 2's stance on THAT claim: agrees, rejects, or accepts part and disputes part (the commonest hard case: "the finding is real, but the explanation is wrong or incomplete"). Traps: a choice that makes Text 2 reject everything when it concedes a point; a choice about something Text 2 never addresses; a choice that states Text 2's own claim more strongly ("proves," "shows") than Text 2 does.
cards.n: Readers who spot Text 2's "But" pick the strongest disagreement choice; the right answer usually keeps Text 2's concession.

cards.q:
Text 1: Many linguists hold that children learn grammar mainly by detecting statistical patterns in speech: given enough input, general-purpose learning explains how toddlers master word order.
Text 2: Statistical learning clearly plays a role: infants track which syllables follow which. But children also produce forms they have never heard, such as "goed" and "mouses," suggesting they apply rules rather than just reproduce what they hear.
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the linguists' view in Text 1?
(A) By denying that infants notice patterns in speech
(B) By agreeing that statistical learning contributes to learning grammar but arguing that it is not the whole explanation
(C) By arguing that children learn grammar more slowly than Text 1 suggests
(D) By agreeing that general-purpose learning fully explains how children learn grammar
cards.a: (B). Text 2 concedes "statistical learning clearly plays a role" and then uses "goed" and "mouses" to argue that pattern-copying is not the whole story. (A) contradicts the concession. (C) is about speed, which Text 2 never discusses. (D) ignores the "But."
cards.n: (A) is the trap for readers who see "But" and assume total disagreement; Text 2's first sentence agrees in part.

cards.q:
Text 1: In a survey led by public health researcher Dana Whitfield, adults who owned dogs walked about 20 more minutes a day than adults who did not. Whitfield concludes that getting a dog increases a person's physical activity.
Text 2: Comparisons of dog owners and non-owners cannot show that dogs cause people to walk more. People who already enjoy walking may be more likely to get a dog in the first place.
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Whitfield's conclusion?
(A) Owning a dog decreases physical activity for most people.
(B) Whitfield's survey overstated how many minutes dog owners walk each day.
(C) The difference Whitfield found may reflect which people choose to own dogs rather than an effect of owning one.
(D) The survey proves that people who enjoy walking are more likely to get dogs.
cards.a: (C). Text 2 accepts the difference but questions the causal conclusion: people who already like walking may be the ones who get dogs. (B) disputes the data, which Text 2 never does. (A) makes a claim Text 2 does not make. (D) is too strong: Text 2 says "may be," and no survey result proves it.
cards.n: (D) states Text 2's alternative as proven; Text 2 only raises a possibility, so the right answer keeps "may."

cards.q:
Text 1: Red markings on the walls of three Spanish caves have been dated, by uranium-thorium analysis of the mineral crusts over them, to more than 64,000 years ago, before modern humans are known to have reached Europe. The markings therefore show that Neanderthals made cave art.
Text 2: Some archaeologists question those dates, arguing that the way the crusts were sampled can make the markings appear older than they are. If the true dates are younger, modern humans could have made the markings.
Based on the texts, how would the archaeologists in Text 2 most likely characterize the conclusion in Text 1?
(A) As showing that Neanderthals and modern humans made art together
(B) As mistaking natural stains for intentional markings
(C) As proving that modern humans reached Europe earlier than believed
(D) As resting on dates that may not be reliable
cards.a: (D). Text 2's objection is to the dating method and so to the dates, on which Text 1's conclusion depends. (B) fails because Text 2 never questions whether the markings are art. (C) and (A) overstate the case: Text 2 says modern humans COULD have made the markings if the dates are younger, not that they did.
cards.n: (B) is a common objection to cave-art claims generally, which is why it sounds right, but Text 2 raises only the dates.

cards.q:
Text 1: Street trees cool cities by shading pavement and releasing water vapor. Planners should plant as many as they can, especially in neighborhoods that lack shade.
Text 2: Trees do lower street temperatures. In arid cities, though, keeping them alive can require heavy irrigation that strains scarce water supplies, so planners there should also consider shade structures such as canopies.
Based on the texts, the authors of both texts would most likely agree with which statement?
(A) Every city should plant as many street trees as it can.
(B) Street trees can lower the temperature of city streets.
(C) Shade structures cool streets more than trees do.
(D) Irrigating trees is the best use of water in arid cities.
cards.a: (B). Text 1 says trees cool cities; Text 2 grants "Trees do lower street temperatures." (A) is Text 1's recommendation, which Text 2 qualifies for arid cities. (C) compares effectiveness, which neither text does. (D) contradicts Text 2's concern about water.
cards.h: → letter + the point both texts state
cards.n: (A) is what Text 1 most wants; a "both would agree" answer must survive Text 2's reservation.

cards.q:
Text 1: In a study by psychologist Lena Brandt, students who took lecture notes by hand scored higher on conceptual questions than students who typed notes. Brandt concludes that handwriting itself deepens understanding.
Text 2: Typists tend to copy a lecture word for word, while handwriters, who cannot keep up, must summarize. In a follow-up study by psychologist Theo Marsh, typists told to summarize instead of copying scored as well as handwriters on conceptual questions.
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Brandt's conclusion?
(A) The score gap is likely real but may come from summarizing, not from handwriting itself.
(B) Brandt's finding is wrong, because typists score higher on conceptual questions.
(C) Handwriting is the most effective way to learn from a lecture.
(D) Students should avoid summarizing lectures.
cards.a: (A). Text 2 accepts the gap (it explains it) but locates its cause in summarizing, since typists who summarized matched handwriters. (B) rejects the finding itself, which Text 2 does not do. (C) repeats Brandt's view. (D) contradicts Text 2, which shows summarizing helps.
cards.h: → letter + the finding vs its explanation
cards.n: (B) mistakes "the explanation is wrong" for "the result is wrong"; Text 2 explains the result, which means it accepts it.

cards.q:
Text 1: In 1993, researchers reported that college students who listened to a Mozart sonata for about ten minutes scored higher on a spatial reasoning task shortly afterward. Popular accounts soon claimed that listening to Mozart makes children smarter.
Text 2: Later studies found the effect small and brief, and it also appeared after people heard other music or stories they enjoyed, suggesting it came from a temporary lift in alertness or mood, not from Mozart.
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the popular accounts described in Text 1?
(A) By agreeing that listening to Mozart has lasting benefits for children
(B) By claiming that the 1993 researchers invented their results
(C) By arguing that the evidence does not show that Mozart's music in particular makes anyone smarter
(D) By arguing that music reduces people's alertness
cards.a: (C). Text 2 finds the effect small, brief and not specific to Mozart, which undercuts the popular claim. (B) accuses the original researchers of fraud; Text 2 accepts that a short-term effect appeared. (A) contradicts "small and brief." (D) reverses Text 2's suggestion of a lift in alertness.
cards.n: Not every cross-text answer is "partly agrees": here Text 2 rejects the popular claim, while (B) overshoots even that into fraud.

cards.q:
Text 1: Island foxes on California's Channel Islands are much smaller than their mainland relatives, the gray fox. Ecologist Paul Varga finds this puzzling: with few competitors on the islands, he argues, the foxes should have grown larger, as some island species have.
Text 2: On small islands, food is limited, and smaller animals need less of it. Many island mammals of medium to large size, from foxes to extinct dwarf mammoths, became smaller over generations.
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Varga's puzzle?
(A) By agreeing that the foxes should have grown larger
(B) By offering a possible explanation for the foxes' small size that Varga does not consider
(C) By arguing that the foxes are not actually smaller than gray foxes
(D) By claiming that the islands have many competitors
cards.a: (B). Text 2 supplies a reason for shrinking (limited food favors smaller bodies) that Varga, focused on competition, leaves out. (A) contradicts that explanation. (C) denies a fact both texts accept. (D) says something Text 2 never mentions.
cards.n: (C) is the "reject everything" choice; Text 2 accepts the size difference and explains it.

cards.q:
Text 1: Critic Hana Osei faults the novel's ending, in which the estranged brothers suddenly reconcile. The change, she argues, is unearned: nothing earlier prepares the reader for it.
Text 2: The reconciliation is quietly foreshadowed. In the first chapter, each brother keeps a copy of the same photograph; midway through, the younger one nearly calls the older, then hangs up.
Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to Osei's criticism?
(A) By arguing that the brothers never actually reconcile
(B) By agreeing that the reconciliation comes without warning
(C) By pointing to earlier details that prepare the reader for the ending
(D) By claiming that the novel's first chapter is its weakest
cards.a: (C). Osei says nothing earlier prepares the ending; Text 2 answers by citing two earlier details (the shared photograph, the nearly made call). (B) contradicts Text 2. (A) denies the ending both texts describe. (D) is an evaluation Text 2 never makes.
cards.n: (A) is tempting if you over-read "quietly"; Text 2 accepts that the brothers reconcile and argues only about preparation.

cards.q: "Which choice best states the main idea of the text?" What separates the main idea from the tempting wrong answers on the hard module?
cards.a: The main idea is the claim that the rest of the text serves; test each choice by asking whether EVERY sentence supports it. Three traps: a true detail from one sentence (often the vivid one, or the opening hook the text goes on to reject); a choice broader than the text (all cities, always, proves); and a choice that states the text's topic without its point. When the text turns ("Until...," "In fact," "But"), the main idea usually lives after the turn.
cards.h: → the test + three traps + where the turn puts it
cards.n: The first sentence is often a view the text sets up to knock down; a choice that restates it is the classic main-idea trap.

cards.q:
"Stone tools found at Lomekwi, in Kenya, have been dated to about 3.3 million years ago. The oldest known fossils of the genus Homo are about 2.8 million years old. Until the Lomekwi discovery, many researchers assumed that toolmaking began with Homo. The find suggests that earlier hominins, perhaps australopithecines, were already shaping stone."
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) The Lomekwi tools are about 3.3 million years old.
(B) Australopithecines were the first hominins to make stone tools.
(C) A discovery in Kenya suggests that stone tools were being made before the genus Homo appeared, challenging an earlier assumption.
(D) The oldest known fossils of the genus Homo are about 2.8 million years old.
cards.a: (C). The text sets out an assumption (toolmaking began with Homo) and reports a find whose age challenges it; every sentence serves that point. (A) and (D) are true details that support it. (B) overstates the text's "perhaps" and adds "first," which the text never claims.
cards.h: → letter + the claim every sentence serves
cards.n: (B) is the most specific-sounding claim; hedges in the text ("suggests," "perhaps") cap how strong the main idea can be.

cards.q:
"It is tempting to credit the Wright brothers' 1903 success to their engine. In fact, the engine was modest, built in their own shop because no suitable one could be bought. What set the brothers apart was their system for controlling an aircraft in the air, including wing-warping to control roll, an idea Wilbur developed partly by watching birds and which the brothers tested on gliders for three years."
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) The Wright brothers built their own engine because none was available for purchase.
(B) The Wright brothers' crucial advance was a system for controlling an aircraft, not engine power.
(C) The Wright brothers' engine was the key to their success in 1903.
(D) Wilbur Wright studied birds to learn how they generate lift.
cards.a: (B). "In fact" rejects the opening idea, and the rest of the text explains what really set the brothers apart: control, especially wing-warping. (C) is the view the text rejects. (A) is a supporting detail. (D) distorts the text: Wilbur watched birds to develop roll control, not to study lift.
cards.n: (C) restates the first sentence; the "tempting" hook is there to be knocked down.

cards.q:
"Ecologist Ana Ruiz surveyed bees in 14 urban parks in Madrid. Parks planted with native shrubs hosted about twice as many bee species as parks planted mainly with lawns and ornamental flowers. Ruiz found that the pattern held regardless of park size."
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) In the parks Ruiz studied, native shrubs were associated with greater bee diversity, whatever the park's size.
(B) Planting native shrubs causes bee diversity to double in every city.
(C) Larger parks host more bee species than smaller parks.
(D) Lawns and ornamental flowers attract no bees.
cards.a: (A). It keeps the text's scope (the 14 parks studied) and its full finding (more bee species with native shrubs, regardless of size). (B) overreaches twice: from association to cause, and from Madrid's parks to every city. (C) contradicts "regardless of park size." (D) overstates "twice as many" into none.
cards.h: → letter + the scope the text actually covers
cards.n: (B) sounds like the headline version; a main idea keeps the study's scope and its "associated with."

cards.q:
"Some historians attribute the unsigned portrait to the painter Maria Kessel, citing its loose brushwork; others credit her teacher, Jan Vos. A 2019 analysis found that the canvas was woven on a type of loom that came into use only after Vos's death. The author concludes that the portrait is far more likely Kessel's than Vos's."
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) Kessel's brushwork closely resembles that of her teacher, Vos.
(B) Looms changed significantly after Vos's death.
(C) Historians have never agreed about who painted most of Kessel's works.
(D) Evidence about the canvas weighs heavily against Vos, so the author attributes the portrait to Kessel.
cards.a: (D). The text lays out two attributions and then uses the canvas evidence to decide between them; that decision is its point. (A) is not stated (only Kessel's brushwork is mentioned). (C) generalizes from one portrait to "most of Kessel's works." (B) is a detail that serves the argument.
cards.h: → letter + the question the text settles
cards.n: (B) is the new fact the text introduces, so it feels central; it matters only as evidence for the attribution.

cards.q:
"Old Anselm had rowed the ferry across the river twice a day for forty years. When the new bridge opened upstream, the town gave him a plaque and a party. The next morning, at the usual hour, he untied the boat and rowed across, empty, and back again. He did the same that evening."
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) Anselm resents the town for building the bridge.
(B) Anselm continues his long routine even after it has lost its practical purpose.
(C) The new bridge was poorly designed, so people still needed the ferry.
(D) Anselm is proud of the plaque the town gave him.
cards.a: (B). The text's point is that Anselm keeps rowing, at the usual hours, though the boat is now empty. (A) invents resentment the text never shows. (C) contradicts "empty": no one needs the ferry. (D) is not supported; the plaque is mentioned only as the town's farewell.
cards.n: (A) is the dramatic reading; the text gives actions, not anger, so resentment is an addition.

cards.q:
"The monarch butterflies that migrate to central Mexico each fall belong to a special generation. Summer monarchs live only two to six weeks, but members of the migrating generation can live eight or nine months, and they delay reproduction until spring, when they begin the journey north."
According to the text, how does the migrating generation differ from summer generations?
(A) It lives much longer and postpones reproduction until spring.
(B) It navigates using the position of the Sun.
(C) It reproduces in central Mexico during the winter.
(D) It completes the round trip to Mexico and back to Canada.
cards.a: (A). The text states both differences: eight or nine months vs two to six weeks, and delayed reproduction. (B) may be true of monarchs but is not in the text, and a detail question asks only what the text says. (C) contradicts "delay reproduction until spring." (D) is never stated.
cards.h: → letter + the sentence that says it
cards.n: (B) is a real fact about monarchs, which is exactly the danger: "According to the text" rules out outside knowledge.

cards.q:
"Critics have long called the composer's late string quartets difficult, even perverse. The difficulty is real: abrupt shifts of tempo interrupt long, slow melodies, and one quartet originally ended with a fugue so dense that early critics called it incomprehensible. Yet listeners who return to the quartets often find that the interruptions come to seem inevitable, as if the music could not have gone any other way."
Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
(A) Although the late quartets are genuinely difficult, repeated listening can make their strangeness seem necessary.
(B) The late quartets are too difficult for most listeners to enjoy.
(C) Early critics called the fugue that originally ended one quartet incomprehensible.
(D) Critics were wrong to call the late quartets difficult.
cards.a: (A). The text grants the difficulty ("The difficulty is real") and then, after "Yet," says repeated listening changes how it is heard. (B) stops before the turn. (C) is a supporting detail. (D) contradicts "The difficulty is real."
cards.n: (D) over-reads the "Yet" as a rebuttal; the text keeps the critics' point and adds to it.

cards.q: "Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researcher's hypothesis?" What must the right finding match, and what are the traps?
cards.a: It must match the hypothesis exactly in (1) subject (the same species, group or place), (2) the specific variable or mechanism claimed (temperature rather than light; reproduction rather than survival), (3) direction (fewer, not more), and (4) scope. It must also separate the claimed cause from the rivals, usually by holding one factor constant. Traps: a finding consistent with the hypothesis that does not isolate its cause, a finding about a related but different subject, and a finding in the wrong direction.
cards.h: → four things to match + what the finding must isolate
cards.n: "Consistent with" is not "supports": a finding that every rival explanation also predicts supports none of them.

cards.q:
"A species of tree frog turns from green to brown each autumn, when both daylight and temperature decline. Biologist Kofi Asante hypothesizes that the change is triggered by falling temperature rather than by shorter days."
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Asante's hypothesis?
(A) Frogs kept at a constant temperature changed color when their daily hours of light were reduced.
(B) In the wild, the frogs change color every autumn.
(C) Frogs kept under constant light changed color when the temperature was lowered, but frogs kept at a constant temperature did not change color when the light was reduced.
(D) A related frog species changes color in response to day length.
cards.a: (C). It separates the two candidate triggers: a temperature drop alone produced the change, and less light alone did not. (A) supports the rival (light). (B) is consistent with both, since both decline in autumn. (D) is about a different species, and points toward light anyway.
cards.h: → letter + which factor is held constant
cards.n: (B) is true and on topic, but when both factors fall together a finding cannot tell them apart.

cards.q:
"Marine ecologist Sofia Brandt claims that warmer water reduces reproduction in a species of sea star."
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Brandt's claim?
(A) More adult sea stars died in warm-water tanks than in cool-water tanks.
(B) In unusually warm years, more sea star larvae were found in the wild than in cool years.
(C) Females in warm-water tanks produced fewer eggs than females in cool-water tanks.
(D) Sea stars in warm-water tanks grew larger than those in cool-water tanks.
cards.a: (C). The claim is about reproduction, and (C) shows reduced egg production in warmer water, in the claimed direction. (A) is about survival, a different variable. (B) points the opposite way (more larvae in warm years). (D) is about growth.
cards.h: → letter + the exact variable in the claim
cards.n: (A) shows that warm water is harmful, which feels close enough; the claim names reproduction, and deaths of adults are not a measure of it.

cards.q:
"Entomologist Rhea Castillo claims that a widely used pesticide reduces the growth of bumblebee colonies."
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Castillo's claim?
(A) Bumblebee colonies exposed to the pesticide produced about 20 percent fewer new workers than unexposed colonies.
(B) Honeybee colonies exposed to the pesticide produced fewer new workers than unexposed colonies.
(C) The pesticide breaks down in soil within a few weeks of application.
(D) Bumblebees exposed to the pesticide visited more flowers per hour than unexposed bees.
cards.a: (A). It measures colony growth (new workers) in bumblebees, comparing exposed and unexposed colonies. (B) is the scope trap: honeybees are a different species. (C) is about the chemical, not the bees. (D) measures foraging, not colony growth, and does not show harm.
cards.n: (B) has the right variable and direction, so it feels like the answer; the claim names bumblebees.

cards.q:
"Economist Priya Nair claims that the downtown parking fee the city introduced in January caused the 15 percent drop in downtown car traffic that followed."
Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Nair's claim?
(A) Downtown businesses reported that fewer customers arrived by car after January.
(B) Downtown car traffic fell by a similar amount that year in nearby cities that did not introduce parking fees.
(C) The fee was the city's first change to its parking rules in a decade.
(D) In a survey, drivers said the fee made them less likely to drive downtown.
cards.a: (B). If traffic fell just as much where there was no fee, something other than the fee probably caused the drop, which undercuts the causal claim. (A) and (D) are consistent with the claim and would support it. (C) is irrelevant to what caused the drop.
cards.h: → letter + what a rival cause looks like
cards.n: (C) sounds like context that matters, but "weaken" needs evidence that the fee did not do it; a comparison group without the fee provides that.

cards.q:
"Ornithologist Lise Moreau hypothesizes that a species of migratory songbird uses Earth's magnetic field to navigate on overcast nights, when the stars are hidden."
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Moreau's hypothesis?
(A) The birds navigated accurately on overcast nights.
(B) On clear nights, the birds navigated accurately using the stars.
(C) On overcast nights, birds fitted with small magnets that disrupt the field around their heads became disoriented, while birds fitted with nonmagnetic brass bars of the same weight did not.
(D) The birds migrated farther in years with fewer overcast nights.
cards.a: (C). It links navigation on overcast nights directly to the magnetic field: disrupting the field caused disorientation, and the brass bars rule out the weight of the device as the cause. (A) shows the birds navigate without stars but not that they use magnetism. (B) is about clear nights. (D) is about distance, not the cue used.
cards.h: → letter + what the control rules out
cards.n: (A) is consistent with the hypothesis, but any non-star cue would explain it; only a manipulation of the field isolates magnetism.

cards.q:
"Historian Omar Haddad claims that an undated letter in a county archive was written after 1850."
Which finding, if true, would most directly support Haddad's claim?
(A) The letter is written on paper from a mill that operated from 1838 to 1861.
(B) The letter describes a trip on a railway line that, according to company records, opened in 1852.
(C) The letter's handwriting matches that of a letter dated 1847.
(D) The letter was found in a box of documents dated from 1845 to 1870.
cards.a: (B). A trip on a line that opened in 1852 could not have been described before 1852, so the letter must be later than 1850. (A) and (D) fit the claim but equally fit a date before 1850. (C) suggests the writer was active in 1847, which does not help place this letter after 1850.
cards.h: → letter + which finding sets a lower limit on the date
cards.n: (A) and (D) have date ranges that overlap the claim, which looks supportive; support needs a date the letter could not precede.

cards.q:
"Robert Frost's poem 'The Road Not Taken' is often read as praise for choosing an unusual path. Some critics note, however, that the poem itself suggests the two roads were nearly identical."
Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates the critics' point?
(A) "Two roads diverged in a yellow wood,"
(B) "Though as for that the passing there / Had worn them really about the same,"
(C) "Because it was grassy and wanted wear;"
(D) "I took the one less traveled by, / And that has made all the difference."
cards.a: (B). The speaker admits the passing feet "Had worn them really about the same," so the roads were nearly identical. (D) is the famous line the popular reading relies on, the opposite of the critics' point. (C) gives the speaker's first reason for choosing, that one road seemed less worn, which he then takes back. (A) only says the roads split.
cards.h: → letter + the line that matches the claim exactly
cards.n: (D) is the line everyone remembers, and it is the one the critics say the poem undercuts; match the claim, not the poem's fame.

cards.q:
"In Emily Dickinson's poem that begins '"Hope" is the thing with feathers,' the speaker suggests that hope asks nothing in return, even in the hardest circumstances."
Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
(A) "'Hope' is the thing with feathers - / That perches in the soul -"
(B) "And sings the tune without the words - / And never stops - at all -"
(C) "And sore must be the storm - / That could abash the little Bird"
(D) "Yet - never - in Extremity, / It asked a crumb - of Me."
cards.a: (D). "In Extremity" is the hardest circumstances, and "never... asked a crumb" is asking nothing in return; both halves of the claim are in the lines. (B) shows that hope is constant, not that it asks nothing. (C) shows it is hard to silence. (A) introduces the metaphor.
cards.h: → letter + both parts of the claim
cards.n: (B) is about hope's persistence, a nearby idea; the claim's specific point is cost, and only (D) mentions asking for anything.

cards.q:
"In William Wordsworth's poem 'I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud,' the speaker suggests that the memory of the daffodils continues to bring him joy long after he saw them."
Which quotation from the poem most effectively illustrates this claim?
(A) "For oft, when on my couch I lie / In vacant or in pensive mood, / They flash upon that inward eye / Which is the bliss of solitude;"
(B) "When all at once I saw a crowd, / A host, of golden daffodils;"
(C) "Continuous as the stars that shine / And twinkle on the milky way,"
(D) "I wandered lonely as a cloud / That floats on high o'er vales and hills,"
cards.a: (A). "Oft" (often), "when on my couch I lie," and "that inward eye" show the daffodils returning in memory long afterward, as a "bliss." (D) and (B) describe the original walk and sighting. (C) describes how many daffodils there were, and "Continuous" refers to their extent, not to the memory lasting.
cards.h: → letter + later memory vs the original scene
cards.n: (C)'s "Continuous" sounds like "continues to bring joy"; it describes the line of flowers stretching along the bay.

cards.q: "Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?" What two tests must the right choice pass, and what do the three standard wrong choices look like?
cards.a: Test 1: every word of the choice is true of the table (each number, each comparison word: "more than twice," "the highest," "every"). Test 2: the choice supports the SPECIFIC claim (the right groups, the right variable, the right comparison, proportion rather than count if the claim is about shares). The standard wrong choices are true but irrelevant; relevant but false in one detail; and relevant and true but about the wrong comparison (counts for a proportion, one group for "every group").
cards.n: Checking only the numbers you read first lets a single false comparison word ("surpassing," "fivefold") slip through.

cards.q:
Wheat yield by variety (tonnes per hectare)
Variety · Normal year · Drought year
Aldra · 6.1 · 3.0
Belmont · 5.4 · 4.3
Corvo · 6.8 · 3.1
Delis · 4.9 · 4.2
An agronomist claims that the varieties with the highest yields in a normal year are not necessarily the best choices for regions prone to drought. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?
(A) Corvo had the highest normal-year yield, 6.8, but one of the lowest drought-year yields, 3.1, while Belmont yielded 4.3 in the drought year.
(B) Delis had the lowest normal-year yield of the four varieties, 4.9.
(C) All four varieties yielded less in the drought year than in a normal year.
(D) Aldra yielded more in the drought year than Belmont did.
cards.a: (A). The claim contrasts normal-year yield with drought performance, and (A) shows the top normal-year variety doing poorly in drought while another does better. (B) and (C) are true but do not connect the two conditions in the way the claim needs. (D) is false: Aldra's 3.0 is less than Belmont's 4.3.
cards.h: → letter + true AND about the claim
cards.n: (C) is true of every row and sounds like a drought finding; it says nothing about whether top normal-year varieties are the best drought choices.

cards.q:
Housing and bird counts at three sites
Site · Housing units added, 2010–2020 · Birds counted, 2010 · Birds counted, 2020
North Marsh · 40 · 520 · 480
East Fields · 310 · 610 · 350
River Bend · 120 · 450 · 380
A student claims that the site that gained the most housing also had the largest decline in birds counted. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?
(A) East Fields had the highest bird count of the three sites in 2010.
(B) North Marsh gained the fewest housing units and had the lowest bird count in 2020.
(C) East Fields gained 310 housing units, the most of any site, and its bird count fell by 260, more than at either other site.
(D) River Bend's bird count fell from 450 to 380.
cards.a: (C). The claim pairs two facts, most housing and largest decline, and (C) gives both for East Fields (a drop of 260 vs 40 at North Marsh and 70 at River Bend). (B) is false: North Marsh's 480 was the highest count in 2020, not the lowest. (A) is true but not about change or housing. (D) is true but about a different site.
cards.h: → letter + both halves of the claim
cards.n: (A) names the right site with a true number, which feels like support; the claim is about the decline, and 2010 alone cannot show it.

cards.q:
Students who bike to school
School · Students surveyed · Students who bike
Alder · 400 · 60
Birch · 150 · 45
Cedar · 250 · 50
A student claims that Birch has the highest proportion of students who bike to school among the three schools. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?
(A) Alder has the largest number of students who bike, 60.
(B) At Birch, 45 of 150 students surveyed bike, 30 percent, compared with 15 percent at Alder and 20 percent at Cedar.
(C) Birch surveyed the fewest students of the three schools.
(D) At Cedar, 50 of 250 students surveyed bike, a larger share than at Birch.
cards.a: (B). A proportion claim needs shares, and (B) computes them: 45/150 = 30%, 60/400 = 15%, 50/250 = 20%. (A) gives a count, which cannot show a proportion (and Alder's count is the largest while its share is the smallest). (C) is true but not about biking. (D) is false: 20% is less than 30%.
cards.n: (A) is the largest number in the "bike" column; counts only answer a proportion claim when the groups are the same size.

cards.q:
Electricity generated in a region (gigawatt-hours)
Year · Solar · Wind
2018 · 120 · 410
2020 · 260 · 450
2022 · 540 · 470
A student claims that the region's solar generation grew rapidly and had overtaken wind generation by 2022. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?
(A) Solar generation more than doubled between 2018 and 2020, surpassing wind generation in 2020.
(B) Solar generation grew more than fivefold between 2018 and 2022.
(C) Wind generation rose from 410 gigawatt-hours in 2018 to 470 in 2022.
(D) Solar generation rose from 120 gigawatt-hours in 2018 to 540 in 2022, exceeding wind's 470 gigawatt-hours that year.
cards.a: (D). It shows rapid growth (120 to 540) and solar exceeding wind in 2022 (540 vs 470), with every figure correct. (A) starts true (120 to 260 is more than double) but is false in its second half: 260 is below wind's 450 in 2020. (B) is false: 540 ÷ 120 = 4.5, not more than 5. (C) is true but about wind alone.
cards.n: (A) and (B) each contain one false word ("surpassing," "fivefold") inside mostly true statements; that single word is the whole question.

cards.q:
A botanical garden has recorded the average date on which its lilacs first bloom. The average was about May 12 in the 1970s and about April 30 in the 2010s. Over the same decades, the garden's average March temperature rose from 4.1°C to 6.0°C.
A student claims that the garden's lilacs now bloom earlier than they did several decades ago. Which choice most effectively uses the data to support the claim?
(A) The garden's average March temperature rose from 4.1°C to 6.0°C.
(B) The lilacs' average first-bloom date moved later, from about April 30 to about May 12.
(C) The lilacs' average first-bloom date moved from about May 12 in the 1970s to about April 30 in the 2010s.
(D) The garden has recorded lilac blooming dates for several decades.
cards.a: (C). The claim is about bloom timing, and (C) shows the date moving about twelve days earlier. (A) is true and may explain the change, but it is about temperature, not blooming. (B) reverses the direction. (D) is true but gives no data.
cards.h: → letter + the variable the claim names
