cards.n: (A) is the likely cause and sounds scientific; the claim asks for evidence of the effect, not its cause.

cards.q:
Average trust in local news sources, by age (1 = none, 5 = complete), from a survey of 1,000 adults in one city
Source · Ages 18–34 · Ages 35–54 · Ages 55 and older
Local TV · 3.1 · 3.4 · 3.9
Newspapers · 3.6 · 3.5 · 3.8
Social media · 2.9 · 2.2 · 1.8
"Older respondents did not trust every source more than younger respondents did. For example, ______"
Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
(A) respondents aged 55 and older gave local TV a 3.9, compared with 3.1 from those aged 18 to 34.
(B) respondents aged 35 to 54 gave newspapers a 3.5.
(C) respondents aged 18 to 34 trusted social media more than local TV.
(D) respondents aged 55 and older gave social media a 1.8, compared with 2.9 from those aged 18 to 34.
cards.a: (D). The claim needs a source that older respondents trusted LESS than younger ones, and social media (1.8 vs 2.9) is one. (A) is true but shows older respondents trusting more, the opposite of what the example must show. (B) is a single number with no comparison. (C) is false (2.9 is less than 3.1) and does not compare age groups anyway.
cards.h: → letter + which direction the example needs
cards.n: (A) is true and shows a clear age gap, so it jumps out; the example must run against the pattern, not with it.

cards.q:
Average reading scores before and after a tutoring program
School · Before · After
Hill · 71 · 78
Lake · 68 · 66
Park · 74 · 80
A district report claims that the tutoring program raised average reading scores at all three schools. Which choice best describes data from the table that weaken this claim?
(A) Park had the highest average score both before and after the program.
(B) Hill's average score rose by 7 points.
(C) Lake's average score rose after the program.
(D) At Lake, the average score fell from 68 before the program to 66 after it.
cards.a: (D). "All three schools" is refuted by a single school where scores fell, and Lake's did. (B) supports the claim for one school. (A) is true but says nothing about change. (C) is false: Lake's average fell.
cards.n: Weaken questions flip the usual direction; students who hunt for support pick (B).

cards.q:
Results of a drug trial (60 participants in each group)
Group · Improved · No change · Worse
Women, drug · 42 · 10 · 8
Women, placebo · 20 · 30 · 10
Men, drug · 25 · 25 · 10
Men, placebo · 22 · 28 · 10
A researcher claims that the drug's benefit appeared mainly among women. Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support the claim?
(A) More women than men improved on the drug, 42 compared with 25.
(B) More men than women improved on placebo, 22 compared with 20.
(C) The same number of men got worse on the drug as on placebo.
(D) Among women, 42 improved on the drug vs 20 on placebo, while among men, 25 improved on the drug vs 22 on placebo.
cards.a: (D). A drug's benefit is the difference from placebo, and (D) compares drug with placebo within each sex: a gap of 22 among women and only 3 among men. (A) compares drug groups without the placebo baseline, so it cannot show a benefit. (C) and (B) are true but do not measure the drug's effect in either sex.
cards.n: (A) is true and points the right way, but without the placebo rows it cannot separate the drug's effect from women simply improving more.

cards.q: "Which choice most logically completes the text?" For an inference, what makes the right choice right, and what are the two wrong-choice types strong students fall for?
cards.a: The right choice MUST be true given the text; it follows from the stated facts with no outside help, and it is often hedged ("does not necessarily," "at least some," "may"). The traps: a choice that COULD be true (plausible, even likely, but not required), and a choice that goes too far (all, only, proves, never). With conditionals, use the contrapositive: "whenever A, B" gives "not B, so not A" but never "B, so A."
cards.h: → must vs could + the conditional rule
cards.n: The plausible choice that "a researcher would probably conclude" is the trap; ask whether the text forces it.

cards.q:
"Materials scientist Jun Park found that a certain cobalt-blue glaze turns green whenever it is fired above 1,200°C. Every bowl excavated from a kiln site near the river still has the glaze in its original blue. It is therefore reasonable to conclude that the bowls ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) were fired at exactly 1,200°C.
(B) were made by a single potter.
(C) were not fired above 1,200°C.
(D) were fired below 1,000°C.
cards.a: (C). "Whenever fired above 1,200°C → green." The bowls are not green, so (by the contrapositive) they were not fired above 1,200°C. (A) and (D) could be true but are not required; any temperature at or below 1,200°C fits. (B) has no support in the text.
cards.n: (D) is a safe-looking specific number; the text only rules out temperatures above 1,200°C, so any narrower claim is a "could be."

cards.q: Same glaze: it turns green whenever it is fired above 1,200°C. At a second site, the bowls are green. Does it follow that they were fired above 1,200°C?
cards.a: No. "Whenever A, then B" says A is sufficient for B, not that it is the only cause. Green bowls might have turned green for some other reason (a different glaze recipe, burial conditions). Concluding A from B is affirming the consequent. The valid move runs only the other way: not green, so not fired above 1,200°C.
cards.h: → yes/no + the logical name for the error
cards.n: The hard module offers this conclusion as a choice, stated confidently; it is the converse, and the converse does not follow.

cards.q:
"Pollen preserved in lake sediments is often used to tell when crops were first grown in a region. At one lake, a research team found no maize pollen in layers older than 1000 CE. However, maize pollen is heavy and rarely travels far from the plant, and the lake lies two kilometers from the nearest land suitable for growing maize. Thus, the absence of maize pollen in the older layers ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) shows that maize was first grown in the region after 1000 CE.
(B) suggests that maize pollen was carried to the lake by rivers after 1000 CE.
(C) proves that the region's farmers grew other crops before 1000 CE.
(D) does not necessarily indicate that maize was not grown in the region before 1000 CE.
cards.a: (D). Since maize pollen rarely travels far and the fields were two kilometers away, pollen would be missing even if maize were grown on the nearest suitable land; the absence proves nothing either way. (A) is the conclusion the "However" sentence undercuts. (C) is not supported. (B) invents a mechanism the text never mentions.
cards.h: → letter + what the "However" does to the evidence
cards.n: (A) is the natural reading of "no pollen"; the text's last facts exist to show why absence of evidence is not evidence of absence here.

cards.q:
"The earliest surviving manuscripts of the poem date from the early 1400s. However, a letter written in 1350 quotes two of the poem's lines and names the poem's title. This suggests that ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) the author of the 1350 letter wrote the poem.
(B) the poem existed by 1350, earlier than any surviving manuscript of it.
(C) the poem was widely read in the early 1400s.
(D) the surviving manuscripts from the 1400s are forgeries.
cards.a: (B). A letter from 1350 that quotes the poem and names it shows the poem existed by then, before the earliest surviving copies. (A) could be true but is not required; quoting a poem does not mean writing it. (C) is not supported by the existence of manuscripts alone. (D) has no basis: early copies can be lost without later ones being fake.
cards.h: → letter + what the letter's date proves
cards.n: (A) is a tempting story; quoting and naming a title is what readers of someone else's poem do.

cards.q:
"In laboratory tests, the eggs of one pond snail species hatched only at water temperatures below 25°C, and the eggs of a second species hatched only above 28°C. In one pond, the water stayed between 20°C and 24°C all season, and biologists later found newly hatched snails of only one of the two species there. The hatchlings were most likely ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) of the second species, since its eggs hatch at higher temperatures.
(B) of the first species, since the pond never reached the temperatures the second species' eggs require.
(C) of a hybrid of the two species.
(D) of both species in equal numbers.
cards.a: (B). The pond stayed between 20°C and 24°C, below 25°C, the range where only the first species' eggs hatch; the second species needs more than 28°C. (A) reverses the ranges. (C) and (D) contradict "only one of the two species."
cards.h: → letter + match the pond's range to each species
cards.n: Two thresholds in one text invite a swap; write each species' range down before choosing.

cards.q:
"Plant physiologist Irene Kowal grew tomato plants with and without a soil fungus. In nitrogen-poor soil, plants with the fungus grew 40 percent taller than plants without it. In nitrogen-rich soil, the two groups grew to the same height. These results suggest that the fungus's benefit to tomato plants ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) comes from nitrogen that the fungus supplies to the roots.
(B) is the same in all soils.
(C) depends on the conditions of the soil.
(D) is harmful in nitrogen-rich soil.
cards.a: (C). The fungus helped in one soil and made no difference in another, so its benefit varies with soil conditions. (A) is a plausible mechanism, but the text never tests it, so it could be true, not must. (B) contradicts the results. (D) goes too far: "the same height" is no effect, not harm.
cards.h: → letter + must be true vs a plausible mechanism
cards.n: (A) is the smart-sounding explanation a biologist might propose; an inference question rewards what the results require, not what might explain them.

cards.q:
"In a study of 30 aging mice, researchers gave some mice a new drug, had some exercise daily, had some do both, and left some untreated. Only the mice that received both the drug and daily exercise showed improved memory. These results suggest that, for these mice, the drug alone ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) worsened memory.
(B) has no effect on memory in any animal.
(C) is less effective than exercise alone.
(D) was not sufficient to improve memory.
cards.a: (D). Mice given only the drug did not improve, so the drug by itself was not enough in this study. (B) generalizes from these mice to every animal. (C) fails because exercise alone also produced no improvement, so neither beat the other. (A) is not stated: no improvement is not worsening.
cards.h: → letter + stay inside the study's scope
cards.n: (B) states the finding as a universal rule; "for these mice" in the stem is the limit the answer must keep.

cards.q:
"Until recently, all known fossils of an extinct group of armored fish came from rocks that formed in the sea. Paleontologist Grace Obi has now described a well-preserved member of the group from rocks that formed at the bottom of a freshwater lake. Obi's find suggests that ______"
Which choice most logically completes the text?
(A) the group may not have been confined to marine environments.
(B) the marine fossils of the group were misidentified.
(C) the group lived only in fresh water.
(D) all armored fish lived in lakes.
cards.a: (A). A group member preserved in lake rocks suggests at least some of the group lived in, or reached, fresh water, so the group may not have been limited to the sea; "may" fits the single find. (C) and (D) overturn the marine evidence entirely. (B) has no support: the new find adds a habitat without casting doubt on the old fossils.
cards.h: → letter + the hedged conclusion one find allows
cards.n: One surprising fossil tempts a sweeping reversal (C); a single find widens the picture, it does not erase the earlier record.

cards.q:
"When the letter came, Tomas read it twice at the kitchen table, folded it into a small square, and put it in his shirt pocket. At supper he talked about the weather, the price of feed, and the neighbor's fence: everything, his sister noticed, except the letter."
Based on the text, what can most reasonably be inferred about Tomas?
(A) He is avoiding discussing the letter.
(B) He did not understand the letter.
(C) The letter contained good news.
(D) His sister wrote the letter.
cards.a: (A). He keeps the letter close, talks about everything else, and his sister notices that the letter is the one topic he skips: he is avoiding it. (B) is not supported; reading it twice suggests attention, not confusion. (C) could be true or false; the text gives no sign of the news. (D) has no support: nothing in the text says who wrote the letter.
cards.h: → letter + what the actions add up to
cards.n: (C) is the kind of "could be" a story invites; the text supports the avoidance, not the letter's contents.

cards.q:
The whole Boundaries domain rests on one test. Which of these can stand alone as a sentence?
(1) its roots reaching nearly 60 meters below the surface
(2) its roots reach nearly 60 meters below the surface
(3) whose roots reach nearly 60 meters below the surface
(4) which sends its roots nearly 60 meters below the surface
cards.a: Only (2). It has a subject (its roots) and a finite verb (reach) and no subordinating word. (1) has only a participle (reaching), so it is a modifier; (3) and (4) open with a relative pronoun, which makes them dependent clauses. Only (2) can stand after a period or a semicolon as a second independent clause; (1), (3) and (4) must attach to a main clause, usually with a comma.
cards.h: → the one that stands alone + what disqualifies each other
cards.n: "Its" and "which" both look like fresh starts; the test is a finite verb with no subordinator, not how the words begin.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The glacier has retreated two kilometers since 1990, its meltwater now feeds a lake that did not exist a generation ago."
cards.a: Comma splice. "Its meltwater now feeds a lake..." has a subject and a finite verb (feeds), so it is an independent clause, and a comma alone cannot join two of them. Fix with a semicolon or period ("since 1990; its meltwater now feeds...") or turn the second part into an absolute phrase: "since 1990, its meltwater now feeding a lake..."
cards.h: → name the error + two ways to fix it
cards.n: "Its meltwater" reads like a modifier, so the comma feels fine; check for a finite verb (feeds vs feeding), not for how the clause starts.

cards.q:
Which is standard, and why?
(A) The vaccine trial was small; however, its results were striking.
(B) The vaccine trial was small, however, its results were striking.
cards.a: (A). "However" is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two independent clauses. Between two complete sentences it needs a semicolon or period before it and a comma after. (B) is a comma splice with "however" in the middle.
cards.n: ", however," looks like the familiar interrupter, but it is one only when both commas sit inside ONE clause: "The trial, however, was small."

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Most of the expedition's instruments failed in the extreme cold. The seismometer ______ recorded data for all eleven weeks."
(A) , however;
(B) , however,
(C) however
(D) ; however,
cards.a: (B). Here "however" interrupts a single clause ("The seismometer recorded data..."), so it takes a comma on each side. (A) and (D) put a semicolon between the subject and its verb; a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides. (C) leaves the interrupter unpunctuated.
cards.n: Having just learned "; however," for two clauses, strong students reach for it here; count the clauses first: there is only one.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Some bacteria thrive at temperatures that would kill most other organisms ______ Thermus aquaticus, first isolated from a hot spring in Yellowstone National Park, grows best at about 70°C."
(A) organisms, for example,
(B) organisms, for example;
(C) organisms for example,
(D) organisms; for example,
cards.a: (D). Both sides are independent clauses, and "for example" is an adverbial phrase, not a conjunction, so the break before it must be a semicolon or period. (A) is a comma splice. (C) fuses two sentences. (B) attaches "for example" to the first clause, the general claim, instead of to the example that follows.
cards.h: → letter + where the clause break falls
cards.n: "For example" feels like a connector; like "however" and "therefore," it cannot join clauses by itself.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The mixture was heated to 90°C, then it was cooled slowly to room temperature."
cards.a: Comma splice. "Then" is an adverb, not a coordinating conjunction, so ", then" cannot join two independent clauses. Fix: "heated to 90°C; then it was cooled..." or "heated to 90°C, and then it was cooled..." or drop the second subject: "heated to 90°C and then cooled slowly."
cards.n: "Then" sounds like "and," so the splice slips past; only for, and, nor, but, or, yet and so can follow a comma to join two clauses.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The river flooded the valley floor every spring ______ the farmers who settled there built their houses on stilts."
(A) spring so
(B) spring; so,
(C) spring, so
(D) spring, so,
cards.a: (C). "So" is a coordinating conjunction here, and a comma plus a coordinating conjunction joins two independent clauses. (A) omits the comma, fusing the clauses. (B) and (D) put a comma after "so," which splits the conjunction from its own clause; (B) also pairs a semicolon with a conjunction.
cards.n: A comma after "so" looks like a pause for breath; no comma follows a coordinating conjunction.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The survey kit included: a GPS unit, a soil corer, and forty sample bags."
cards.a: Delete the colon: "The survey kit included a GPS unit, a soil corer, and forty sample bags." What comes BEFORE a colon must be a complete sentence, and "The survey kit included" is not one (the verb still needs its object). Alternatively complete it first: "The survey kit included three items: a GPS unit..."
cards.h: → the fix + the rule about what precedes a colon
cards.n: A list feels as if it needs a colon; the rule is about the words before the colon, not after it. The same goes for "such as:" and "including:".

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The expedition had a single aim ______ to find the source of the river before the rains began."
(A) aim;
(B) aim:
(C) aim, it was
(D) aim, and
cards.a: (B). The first part is a complete sentence, and what follows explains it without being a clause of its own, which is exactly a colon's job. (A) fails because "to find the source..." is not an independent clause, and a semicolon needs one on each side. (C) is a comma splice. (D) joins a clause to a fragment with "and."
cards.n: The semicolon looks formal and "correct"; it needs a complete sentence AFTER it too, and an infinitive phrase is not one.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Tardigrades can survive conditions that kill almost every other animal ______ they can lose nearly all of their body water, shut down their metabolism, and revive when they are rehydrated."
(A) animal, and, they
(B) animal, they
(C) animal they
(D) animal: they
cards.a: (D). Both parts are independent clauses and the second explains the first, so a colon joins them (a semicolon or period would also be standard). (B) is a comma splice, (C) a fused sentence, and (A) wrongly puts a comma after "and," splitting the conjunction from its clause.
cards.h: → letter + why the second part may follow a colon
cards.n: Strong students sometimes think a colon must introduce a list; it can introduce any explanation, including a full clause.

cards.q: Right or wrong? "The museum's new wing was designed around a single idea—natural light."
cards.a: Right. A single dash can do a colon's job: after a complete sentence, it introduces the word or phrase that explains or completes it. "A single idea: natural light" would also be standard. A single dash is wrong only when what precedes it cannot stand alone, or when it is meant to close an element opened by a comma.
cards.h: → right/wrong + what a single dash may do
cards.n: Students who know dashes come in pairs mark every lone dash wrong; a lone dash at the end of a complete sentence is fine.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The Voynich manuscript—written on vellum that has been radiocarbon-dated to the early fifteenth century, has never been convincingly deciphered."
cards.a: The element opened with a dash must be closed with a dash: "...to the early fifteenth century—has never been convincingly deciphered." Paired punctuation around a nonessential element must match: dash–dash or comma–comma, never dash–comma. Test: lift out the element between the marks and the sentence still reads "The Voynich manuscript has never been convincingly deciphered."
cards.n: The comma sits exactly where a pause belongs, so it looks right; check what mark OPENED the interruption.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The chemist, Rosalind Franklin, used X-ray diffraction to produce images of DNA."
cards.a: Delete both commas: "The chemist Rosalind Franklin used..." A title or description placed before a name is restrictive (the name tells us which chemist), so it takes no commas. Commas are right when the description follows a name that already identifies the person: "Rosalind Franklin, a chemist, used..."
cards.n: Commas around the name look balanced and careful, and that is why this is a hard-module favorite; the SAT consistently treats "the chemist Rosalind Franklin" as restrictive.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "Wangari Maathai, founder of Kenya's Green Belt Movement became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize, in 2004."
cards.a: Add a comma after "Movement." The name already identifies her, so "founder of Kenya's Green Belt Movement" is a nonessential appositive and must be closed as it was opened: "Wangari Maathai, founder of Kenya's Green Belt Movement, became..." Without the second comma, the subject is cut off from its verb.
cards.h: → where the missing mark goes + why
cards.n: The final ", in 2004" draws the eye; the real error is the unclosed appositive earlier in the sentence.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The bridge's final design, which the engineers revised four times; uses a single suspension cable anchored on the western bank."
cards.a: Replace the semicolon with a comma. The comma after "design" opens a nonessential clause, so a comma must close it; a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides, and "The bridge's final design, which the engineers revised four times" is not one.
cards.h: → the fix + why a semicolon cannot close it
cards.n: The semicolon sits where a strong pause falls; pauses do not decide punctuation, clause structure does.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The fossils that the team recovered from the lowest layer of the quarry, are the oldest known from the region."
cards.a: Delete the comma. Nothing separates a subject from its verb, however long the subject. The subject is "The fossils that the team recovered from the lowest layer of the quarry"; the verb is "are." (Commas could appear only as a pair around a nonessential element, and there is none here.)
cards.h: → the fix + subject and verb named
cards.n: A long subject creates a natural breath before the verb, and that breath tempts a comma; the SAT hides this error behind the longest subjects it can write.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The survey revealed, that most commuters would pay a higher fare for faster service."
cards.a: Delete the comma: "The survey revealed that most commuters would pay..." The that-clause is the object of "revealed," and no punctuation separates a verb from its object or complement.
cards.n: "That" feels like the start of a new idea, so a comma looks natural; it starts the object, not a new clause.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The bridge, that collapsed at Washington's Tacoma Narrows in 1940 had been open for only four months."
cards.a: Delete the comma: "The bridge that collapsed at Washington's Tacoma Narrows in 1940 had been open..." A that-clause is restrictive and never takes commas; here the lone comma also cuts the subject off from its verb. (A nonessential version would use "which" and two commas.)
cards.n: One comma after "bridge" looks like the start of an aside; "that" never begins an aside.

cards.q:
The notice should say that only students who enrolled after May 1 must file the new form. Which version says that?
(A) Students, enrolled after May 1, must file the new form.
(B) Students enrolled after May 1 must file the new form.
cards.a: (B). Without commas, "enrolled after May 1" is restrictive: it identifies which students must file. With commas, (A) treats the phrase as extra information about all students, so it says every student must file (and happens to have enrolled after May 1).
cards.h: → letter + what the commas do to the meaning
cards.n: The commas look tidy, so students pick them by ear; a restrictive modifier is part of the subject's identity and takes none.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The touring exhibition will stop in Lagos, Nigeria, Accra, Ghana, and Dakar, Senegal."
cards.a: Use semicolons between the items: "Lagos, Nigeria; Accra, Ghana; and Dakar, Senegal." When list items contain their own commas, semicolons separate the items, so the reader can tell three cities from six places.
cards.h: → the fix + when a list takes semicolons
cards.n: Every comma is individually "correct" (city, country), so the sentence passes a quick read; count the items.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The panel's three judges were Amara Osei, a sculptor ______ Dev Mehta, a novelist; and Lena Park, a composer."
(A) sculptor;
(B) sculptor,
(C) sculptor:
(D) sculptor—
cards.a: (A). Each item has an internal comma (name, role), and the list already uses a semicolon before "and Lena Park," so items must be separated by semicolons throughout. (B) blurs the items into six names and roles. (C) and (D) introduce explanations and cannot separate list items.
cards.h: → letter + the clue elsewhere in the sentence
cards.n: A comma is the default list mark; the semicolon later in the sentence tells you the list's separator.

cards.q:
Which is standard?
(A) The team sampled the sediment at forty sites, and sent the cores to a lab in Oslo.
(B) The team sampled the sediment at forty sites and sent the cores to a lab in Oslo.
cards.a: (B). "Sent" shares the subject "the team," so there is one clause with two verbs (a compound predicate), and no comma goes before "and." A comma plus "and" joins two independent clauses: "The team sampled the sediment, and a lab in Oslo analyzed the cores."
cards.n: A comma before "and" feels like a natural pause; with no new subject after "and," the SAT marks it wrong.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "Although the probe's orbit remained stable; its instruments drifted out of calibration within a year."
cards.a: Use a comma: "Although the probe's orbit remained stable, its instruments drifted..." "Although..." is a dependent clause, and a semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. A dependent clause attaches to its main clause with a comma.
cards.h: → the fix + why the semicolon fails
cards.n: Both halves are long and have verbs, so they feel like two sentences; the subordinator "although" makes the first one dependent.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "Halley's comet, which Edmond Halley observed in 1682 and whose return he predicted for 1758."
cards.a: A fragment: the subject "Halley's comet" never gets a main verb, because everything after it is a nonessential relative clause. Rewrite as a sentence, e.g. "Edmond Halley observed the comet in 1682 and predicted its return for 1758," or give the subject a verb after the clause: "Halley's comet, which Edmond Halley observed in 1682, now bears his name."
cards.h: → name the error + a repaired sentence
cards.n: The sentence is long and full of verbs (observed, predicted), but they are inside the "which" clause; the hard module builds whole fragments this way.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: "The archivist wondered whether the letter's watermark could date it more precisely than the handwriting could?"
cards.a: End with a period. The sentence reports a question (an indirect question, "wondered whether...") but is itself a statement. A question mark belongs only to a direct question: "Could the watermark date the letter more precisely than the handwriting?"
cards.h: → the fix + direct vs indirect question
cards.n: "Whether" and the questioning content pull toward a question mark; ask whether the sentence itself asks anything.

cards.q: Fix it, or say it is right: The critic argued that, "the novel's final chapter undoes everything the first eleven built."
cards.a: Delete the comma after "that." A quotation worked into the sentence with "that" is the object of the verb, so no comma separates it (and it keeps its lowercase opening). The comma and capital belong to a direct speech tag instead: The critic argued, "The novel's final chapter undoes..."
cards.h: → the fix + integrated vs introduced quotation
cards.n: A quotation seems to demand a comma before it; after "that," it does not.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"In 1846, Johann Galle located Neptune within about one degree of the position that Urbain Le Verrier had calculated ______ it was the first planet found by mathematical prediction rather than by a telescope survey."
(A) calculated, it
(B) calculated it
(C) calculated; it
(D) calculated: and it
cards.a: (C). "It was the first planet..." is an independent clause, so the break needs a semicolon (or period). (A) is a comma splice. (B) fuses the sentences and reads as if Le Verrier "calculated it." (D) follows a colon with "and," which leaves the colon joining a clause to a conjunction.
cards.n: The long first clause wears readers out, and a comma feels like enough; the second part has "it was," a full clause.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The collection of letters, diaries, and photographs that archivists at the historical society catalogued over the past decade ______ now available to researchers online."
(A) is
(B) are
(C) were
(D) have been
cards.a: (A). The subject is "collection," which is singular; "of letters, diaries, and photographs" is a prepositional phrase and "that archivists... catalogued over the past decade" is a relative clause, and neither changes the subject's number. "Now" calls for the present. (B), (C) and (D) are plural, matching the nearby nouns instead of the subject.
cards.n: Three plural nouns and "archivists" sit right before the blank; strike every phrase and clause to find the head noun.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Beneath the ruins of the medieval chapel ______ the foundations of a much older Roman villa, discovered when a drainage trench was dug in 2011."
(A) lies
(B) lie
(C) lying
(D) has lain
cards.a: (B). The order is inverted: the subject, "the foundations," comes after the verb, and it is plural. (A) and (D) are singular, agreeing with "chapel" (or the later "villa"). (C) is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have no main verb.
cards.h: → letter + find the subject after the verb
cards.n: In inverted order, the noun before the blank (chapel) is inside a prepositional phrase; the subject is waiting after the verb.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Among the objects recovered from the shipwreck off the coast of Crete ______ a bronze astrolabe, still legible after centuries in salt water."
(A) was
(B) were
(C) have been
(D) being
cards.a: (A). Inverted order again: the subject is "a bronze astrolabe," singular, and it follows the verb. "Recovered" sets the past. (B) and (C) are plural, agreeing with "objects," which sits inside the prepositional phrase "Among the objects." (D) leaves the sentence with no finite verb.
cards.h: → letter + the subject after the verb
cards.n: "Objects" is the only noun before the blank, so the plural feels automatic; in inversion, look after the verb.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"After two days of deliberation, the jury ______ that the company was not liable for the damage."
(A) has concluded
(B) have concluded
(C) conclude
(D) were concluding
cards.a: (A). In American English, which the SAT follows, a collective noun acting as one body takes a singular verb: the jury has concluded. (B), (C) and (D) treat "jury" as plural.
cards.n: A jury is twelve people, so a plural verb feels logical; the SAT treats jury, team, committee, band and company as singular.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Neither the study's lead author nor her two coauthors ______ willing to comment on the retraction."
(A) was
(B) were
(C) is
(D) has been
cards.a: (B). With "neither... nor" (and "either... or"), the verb agrees with the nearer subject, here the plural "coauthors." Past tense matches the reported event. (A), (C) and (D) are singular, agreeing with "author."
cards.n: "Neither" sounds singular, as in "neither of them was," but with "nor" the nearer subject decides.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The mayor, along with three members of the city council, ______ to attend the opening of the new ferry terminal on Saturday."
(A) plan
(B) plans
(C) are planning
(D) have planned
cards.a: (B). "Along with three members of the city council" is an interrupting phrase; it does not join the subject the way "and" would. The subject is "the mayor," singular. (A), (C) and (D) are plural.
cards.h: → letter + what "along with" does to the subject
cards.n: Four people are going, so a plural feels right; "along with," "as well as" and "together with" never make a subject plural.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The number of bird species recorded at the reservoir ______ since the surrounding wetland was restored in 2016."
(A) have doubled
(B) are doubling
(C) double
(D) has doubled
cards.a: (D). "The number" is singular (it is one quantity), and "since 2016" calls for the present perfect: has doubled. Contrast "A number of species have returned," where "a number of" means "several" and takes a plural verb. (A), (C) and (B) are plural, and (C) and (B) also ignore the "since" cue.
cards.n: "Species" is the nearest noun and is plural; "the number of" is singular whatever follows it.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Measuring the drift of icebergs from satellite images ______ corrections for cloud cover and for the curvature of the Earth."
(A) require
(B) have required
(C) requiring
(D) requires
cards.a: (D). The subject is the gerund phrase "Measuring the drift of icebergs from satellite images," and a gerund subject is singular. (A) and (B) are plural, agreeing with "icebergs" or "images." (C) is not a finite verb, so the sentence would have none.
cards.n: "Images" sits right before the blank; a gerund phrase as subject counts as one activity.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The research consortium, made up of eleven universities and four national laboratories, released ______ first report on coastal erosion in 2021."
(A) their
(B) it's
(C) its
(D) they're
cards.a: (C). The antecedent is "consortium," a singular noun, so the possessive pronoun is "its." (A) agrees with "universities" and "laboratories," which sit inside a modifying phrase. (B) means "it is" and (D) means "they are."
cards.n: Eleven universities feel like "their"; a pronoun agrees with its antecedent's grammatical number, not with how many members it has.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Each of the three orchestras revised ______ program after the guest conductor withdrew from the festival."
(A) its
(B) their
(C) it's
(D) there
cards.a: (A). "Each" is singular, so the pronoun that refers back to it is singular: each... revised its program. (B) agrees with "orchestras," the object of "of." (C) is the contraction of "it is." (D) is an adverb of place.
cards.n: "Three orchestras" is plural, but the subject is "each," and the pronoun follows the subject.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"An octopus can change the color of ______ skin in a fraction of a second, a feat made possible by specialized cells called chromatophores."
(A) its
(B) it's
(C) its'
(D) their
cards.a: (A). The possessive of "it" is "its," with no apostrophe. (B) is "it is," which makes no sense here. (C) is not a word. (D) is plural, but the antecedent is "an octopus."
cards.n: Every other possessive takes an apostrophe, so "it's" looks possessive; test by expanding it to "it is."

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Three field crews surveyed the same marsh in different seasons, each counting nesting pairs of rails. The ______ counts differed by less than five percent, which suggested that the population was stable."
(A) crew's
(B) crews'
(C) crews
(D) crews's
cards.a: (B). The counts belong to the crews (possession), and there are three of them (plural), so the form is plural possessive: crews'. (A) is singular possessive, one crew. (C) is plural with no possession. (D) is not a standard form for a plural ending in s.
cards.n: Ask the two questions separately: how many crews (three, so plural) and do they own the counts (yes, so possessive). Skipping the first gives crew's.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"In winter, the ______ in a honeybee colony cluster together and shiver their flight muscles, keeping the queen at the center of the cluster warm."
(A) bee's
(B) bees'
(C) bees's
(D) bees
cards.a: (D). The word is the plural subject of "cluster"; nothing belongs to the bees in this position, so no apostrophe. (A) and (B) are possessives, which would need a noun after them to own. (C) is not standard.
cards.n: After drilling possessives, students add apostrophes by reflex; a possessive must be followed by the thing it owns.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The exhibit traces the history of the ______ suffrage movement in New Zealand, which in 1893 became the first self-governing country to grant women the right to vote in national elections."
(A) women's
(B) womens'
(C) womens
(D) woman's
cards.a: (A). "Women" is already plural, so its possessive adds 's: women's. (B) and (C) treat "womens" as a word, which it is not. (D) is the possessive of one woman.
cards.n: The rule "plural possessive = s'" tempts womens'; it applies only to plurals ending in s. Children's, people's and men's work like women's.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"By the time Howard Florey and Ernst Chain began purifying penicillin in the late 1930s, Alexander Fleming ______ about the mold's antibacterial effect for roughly a decade."
(A) knows
(B) has known
(C) will have known
(D) had known
cards.a: (D). "By the time... began" sets a past moment, and Fleming's knowing started earlier and continued up to it, which is the past perfect: had known. (A) is present. (B), the present perfect, runs up to now, not to a past moment. (C) is future.
cards.n: "Has known" sounds right with "for roughly a decade," but the reference point is the 1930s, not the present.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Since the city began charging a fee for plastic bags in 2019, the number of bags collected from its storm drains ______ by more than half."
(A) fell
(B) had fallen
(C) has fallen
(D) will fall
cards.a: (C). "Since" plus a past starting point describes a change that runs from then up to now: the present perfect, "has fallen." (A), the simple past, would fit a finished period ("in 2020, the number fell"). (B) needs a later past reference point, and (D) is future.
cards.n: "In 2019" pulls toward the simple past; the word "since" makes the period run to the present.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"In the novel's final chapter, the narrator returns to her grandmother's farm and ______ that the orchard where she played as a child has been cut down."
(A) discovered
(B) would discover
(C) had discovered
(D) discovers
cards.a: (D). The sentence narrates the novel in the present tense ("returns," "has been cut down"), the standard way to describe a literary work, so the parallel verb is "discovers." (A), (C) and (B) shift into past forms in the middle of a present-tense account.
cards.h: → letter + the tense the sentence already uses
cards.n: The events feel past because they happen in a story; follow the tense the sentence sets, not the story's timeline.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"When the power failed at 2:10 a.m., the laboratory's freezers ______ tissue samples from more than 400 patients."
(A) store
(B) will store
(C) were storing
(D) have stored
cards.a: (C). The freezers' storing was ongoing at the past moment the power failed, which is the past progressive: were storing. (A) is present, (B) future, and (D) the present perfect, which ties the action to now rather than to 2:10 a.m. on the night of the failure.
cards.h: → letter + the aspect the time cue calls for
cards.n: "Have stored" sounds formal and complete, but a single past moment ("when the power failed") calls for a past form.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The Rosetta Stone, found in 1799 by French soldiers near the town of Rashid in Egypt, ______ the same decree in hieroglyphic, Demotic, and ancient Greek script."
(A) records
(B) recording
(C) which records
(D) having recorded
cards.a: (A). The subject "The Rosetta Stone" needs a main verb, and "found in 1799... in Egypt" is only a modifier. "Records" supplies the finite verb. (C) turns the rest into a relative clause, (B) and (D) into participial phrases, and all three leave the sentence with no main verb.
cards.h: → letter + does the sentence have a main verb yet?
cards.n: The participle "found" feels like the verb; it is part of a modifier set off by commas, so the main verb is still missing.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"In July 2015, the New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto, ______ images that revealed plains of frozen nitrogen and mountains of water ice."
(A) it returned
(B) returned
(C) and it returning
(D) returning
cards.a: (D). The sentence already has its main verb ("flew"), so after the comma it needs a modifier, and the participial phrase "returning images..." supplies one. (A) creates a comma splice. (B) strings a second verb after a comma without "and." (C) pairs "and it" with a participle, which is ungrammatical.
cards.n: Students who just learned to hunt for a missing main verb choose a finite verb every time; check first whether the sentence already has one.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Having analyzed more than 300 soil samples from the valley, ______"
(A) the results showed that the contamination came from a single source.
(B) the researchers concluded that the contamination came from a single source.
(C) a single source of the contamination was identified by the researchers.
(D) the conclusion of the researchers was that the contamination came from a single source.
cards.a: (B). An introductory modifier describes the noun right after the comma, so that noun must be whoever did the analyzing: the researchers. (A) says the results analyzed the samples, (C) says the source did, and (D) says the conclusion did.
cards.h: → letter + who did the action in the modifier
cards.n: (C) mentions the researchers and sounds formal, but they arrive at the end; the doer must come immediately after the comma.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"A pioneer of early portrait photography, ______"
(A) Julia Margaret Cameron's portraits were deliberately soft in focus.
(B) Julia Margaret Cameron deliberately made her portraits soft in focus.
(C) the portraits made by Julia Margaret Cameron were deliberately soft in focus.
(D) soft focus was used deliberately by Julia Margaret Cameron in her portraits.
cards.a: (B). The appositive "A pioneer of early portrait photography" must describe the noun right after the comma, and only Cameron can be a pioneer. (A) is the hard trap: the subject there is "portraits"; "Cameron's" is only a possessive modifying it. (C) makes the portraits the pioneer, and (D) makes soft focus the pioneer.
cards.h: → letter + what the opening phrase describes
cards.n: (A) puts her name first, so it looks right; a possessive noun cannot be the thing an introductory modifier describes.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"The grant will allow the museum to digitize its photograph collection, ______ its textile storage rooms, and to hire two conservators."
(A) renovating
(B) the renovation of
(C) to renovate
(D) it will renovate
cards.a: (C). Items in a series must share a form, and the other two items are infinitives: "to digitize" and "to hire." So the middle one is "to renovate." (A) is a participle, (B) a noun phrase, and (D) a full clause, each breaking the parallel series.
cards.h: → letter + the form of the other items
cards.n: Reading only the words around the blank, "renovating its textile storage rooms" sounds fine; look at the whole list.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"In summer, the lifespan of a worker honeybee is far shorter than ______, which can live for several years."
(A) a queen
(B) queens
(C) that of a queen
(D) those of queens
cards.a: (C). A comparison must set like against like: the worker's lifespan against the queen's lifespan. "That of a queen" means "the lifespan of a queen." (A) and (B) compare a lifespan with a bee. (D) uses the plural "those" for the singular "lifespan."
cards.n: (A) is what people say out loud, so it sounds natural; the SAT counts comparing a lifespan with a queen as illogical.

cards.q:
Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
"Joy Harjo, ______ appointment as the twenty-third Poet Laureate of the United States was announced in June 2019, was the first Native American to hold the position."
(A) who's
(B) who
(C) whose
(D) her
cards.a: (C). The word must be a possessive relative pronoun: the appointment is Harjo's, and the clause must attach to her name. (A) means "who is," which makes no sense before "appointment." (B) cannot show possession. (D) creates a new clause inside the sentence without joining it, leaving a run-on.
cards.n: "Who's" sounds identical and looks like a possessive; expand it to "who is" to hear the error.

cards.q: What is the reliable method for a transition question at hard-module difficulty, and where does it usually go wrong?
cards.a: Cover the choices. Read the sentence before the blank AND the one after, and name their relation in your own words: despite (concession), but (contrast), because/so (cause), for example, also (addition), same (similarity), before/after or at the same time (sequence), more than that (emphasis), that is (restatement). Only then look at the choices and take the one that names that relation. The hard versions put the real relation two sentences back, or place a negative word ("only," "not merely") where there is no contrast.
cards.h: → the steps in order + the usual failure
cards.n: Trying each choice in the blank "by ear" makes three of them sound fine; name the relation before you look.

cards.q: Sort each transition into the relation it signals: nonetheless, hence, conversely, furthermore, subsequently, indeed, that is, for instance, likewise, meanwhile, instead, specifically.
cards.a: nonetheless → concession (despite that); hence → cause/result; conversely → contrast (the reverse case); furthermore → addition; subsequently → sequence (later); indeed → emphasis (more than that); that is → restatement; for instance → example; likewise → similarity; meanwhile → simultaneity (at the same time); instead → replacement (not that, this); specifically → specification (exactly how).
cards.n: Meanwhile, instead and specifically are the ones strong students misfile, as contrast, contrast and example.

cards.q:
"Admittedly, the survey reached only 212 households, a small sample for a city of two million people. ______ its central finding, that rents rose fastest in neighborhoods near new transit stations, matches the pattern in five years of city permit data."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Therefore,
(B) For instance,
(C) Nevertheless,
(D) Similarly,
cards.a: (C). "Admittedly" concedes a weakness; the next sentence says the finding holds up anyway. That concede-then-counter relation is what nevertheless (or even so, still) signals. (A) would mean the small sample caused the finding to match the permit data. (B) is wrong because the finding is not an example of a small sample, and (D) because it is not a parallel case.
cards.h: → letter + the relation in two words
cards.n: "Therefore" feels like the conclusion-word a strong argument needs; ask whether sentence 1 CAUSES sentence 2. It does not; the finding holds despite it.

cards.q:
"The pilot study enrolled only 24 patients, too few to show whether the drug's modest benefit was real or a product of chance. ______ the research team is now recruiting 600 patients for a second, larger trial."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) However,
(B) Nevertheless,
(C) By contrast,
(D) Accordingly,
cards.a: (D). The small sample is the REASON for the larger trial: sentence 2 is the response that sentence 1 calls for, a cause-and-effect relation. (A) and (B) would mean the team is recruiting despite the weakness, but the weakness is why they are recruiting. (C) compares two different subjects, and there is only one here.
cards.n: A weakness in sentence 1 primes students for a turn ("however"); here the next step follows from the weakness instead of pushing against it.

cards.q:
"Because the island's lizards had lived without predators for thousands of years, biologists expected them to have lost their escape behaviors. ______ when researchers approached the lizards in the field, most fled at about the same distance as lizards on predator-rich islands."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Therefore,
(B) Similarly,
(C) However,
(D) Specifically,
cards.a: (C). Sentence 1 states an expectation; sentence 2 reports a result that goes against it, a contrast. (A) would mean the expectation caused the lizards to flee. (B) would need a parallel case. (D) would need sentence 2 to spell out the expectation more precisely, but it contradicts it.
cards.n: "Because" in sentence 1 plants a cause-and-effect frame; the blank relates the result to the EXPECTATION, and they clash.

cards.q:
"Some songbirds change their songs in response to urban noise. ______ great tits in several European cities sing at higher pitches than great tits in nearby forests, which helps their songs carry above the low rumble of traffic."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) In addition,
(B) For instance,
(C) Nevertheless,
(D) Instead,
cards.a: (B). Sentence 1 is a general claim (some songbirds change their songs); sentence 2 gives one specific case of it (great tits raising their pitch). (A) would mean sentence 2 adds a separate point, but it illustrates the same one. (C) signals a contrast that is not there, and (D) a replacement.
cards.n: "In addition" sounds safe because sentence 2 brings new details; new details about the SAME claim make an example, not an addition.

cards.q:
"Some songbirds in noisy cities sing at higher pitches than rural members of their species, which helps their songs carry above the rumble of traffic. ______ some European robins living in noisy parts of cities sing at night, when the streets are quieter."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) For example,
(B) In addition,
(C) Therefore,
(D) Nevertheless,
cards.a: (B). Sentence 1 describes one response to noise (raising pitch); sentence 2 adds a different one (shifting to night). (A) fails because singing at night is not an instance of singing at a higher pitch. (C) fails because pitch-raising does not cause robins to sing at night, and (D) because nothing is conceded.
cards.h: → letter + is sentence 2 a case of sentence 1?
cards.n: Robins are a specific bird, so "for example" looks right; an example must be a case of the specific claim just made (higher pitch), not just of the topic.

cards.q:
"Without wheeled vehicles or large draft animals, the Inca moved goods across the Andes on the backs of llamas and relied on relay runners to carry messages along their road network. ______ the Aztecs, who had no draft or pack animals at all, supplied their island capital, Tenochtitlan, largely by canoe and by human porters."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Moreover,
(B) Similarly,
(C) Therefore,
(D) Instead,
cards.a: (B). Sentence 2 turns to a DIFFERENT society facing the same limitation and likewise working around it without wheels or draft animals: a parallel case, which similarly (or likewise) signals. (A) adds another point about the same subject or argument, not a parallel case in another society. (C) implies the Inca's methods caused the Aztecs'. (D) implies the Aztecs' method replaced the Inca's.
cards.h: → letter + parallel case or additional point?
cards.n: "Moreover" is the near-miss: it adds a further point about the SAME subject; a new subject behaving the same way calls for similarly or likewise.

cards.q:
"The proposed stadium would require clearing twelve acres of the city's last remaining wetland. ______ the city's own traffic study projects that the stadium would add forty minutes to commutes along the river corridor on game days."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Moreover,
(B) Similarly,
(C) For example,
(D) Nevertheless,
cards.a: (A). Both sentences give reasons to object to the same proposal; sentence 2 adds a second, different drawback, which is what moreover (or furthermore, in addition) signals. (B) would mark a parallel case, a different subject behaving the same way. (C) fails because traffic delay is not an instance of clearing wetland. (D) signals a concession, and nothing in sentence 2 pushes against sentence 1.
cards.h: → letter + one subject, a second reason
cards.n: Two drawbacks feel "similar," but similarly compares two subjects; stacking reasons about one subject is addition.

cards.q: A transition question offers (A) Similarly, (B) Likewise, (C) However, (D) For example. Before reading the passage, what can you conclude, and why?
cards.a: Almost certainly neither (A) nor (B) is the answer. They signal exactly the same relation, so if one fit, the other would too, and a sound question has only one right answer. The same goes for pairs like therefore/thus, however/nevertheless when both would fit a contrast, and in addition/moreover. Still confirm by naming the relation from the passage before choosing between (C) and (D).
cards.n: Treat this as a tiebreaker, not a substitute for reading: occasionally two near-synonyms differ in the relation they signal (however vs nevertheless in a pure comparison).

cards.q:
"The drought did not merely reduce the region's harvest. ______ in the three worst-affected provinces, it destroyed the crop entirely."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Similarly,
(B) However,
(C) In fact,
(D) Consequently,
cards.a: (C). Sentence 2 goes further in the same direction as sentence 1 (not merely reduced, but destroyed), which is emphasis: in fact or indeed. (B) is tempting because of "not merely," but sentence 2 does not contradict sentence 1; it intensifies it. (A) would need a parallel case, and (D) would mean reducing the harvest caused its destruction.
cards.n: The negative "not merely" makes the ear expect "however"; "not merely X... in fact Y" is an intensifier pattern.

cards.q:
"The city's engineers decided not to raise the old seawall with another layer of concrete. ______ they planted a broad strip of salt marsh in front of it, expecting the grasses to absorb wave energy before it reached the wall."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) For example,
(B) Similarly,
(C) Instead,
(D) Moreover,
cards.a: (C). Sentence 1 rules out one option; sentence 2 gives the option chosen in its place, which is what instead (or rather) signals. (D) would add the marsh to the concrete, but there is no concrete. (B) would need a parallel action, and (A) an instance of not raising the wall.
cards.n: After a sentence saying what did NOT happen, "moreover" reads as if both things happened; the replacement relation needs instead.

cards.q:
"The first survey team spent June and July mapping the upper chambers of the cave. ______ a second team, working from an entrance on the far side of the ridge, was surveying the flooded passages below; the two teams met in the middle at the end of July."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) As a result,
(B) Subsequently,
(C) For example,
(D) Meanwhile,
cards.a: (D). The two teams worked during the same period: "was surveying" describes ongoing action, and the teams "met in the middle at the end of July." Meanwhile signals simultaneity. (B) puts the second team's work after the first's, contradicting the meeting. (C) and (A) would make the second team an instance or a result of the first team's work.
cards.n: Order on the page is not order in time; "subsequently" is the trap whenever two actions are reported one after another.

cards.q:
"In 1953, Scott Crossfield became the first pilot to fly at twice the speed of sound. ______ in 1947, Chuck Yeager had become the first pilot confirmed to exceed the speed of sound in level flight."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Subsequently,
(B) Previously,
(C) For example,
(D) As a result,
cards.a: (B). Sentence 2 describes an earlier event: 1947 comes before 1953, and "had become" is past perfect. (A) reverses the order. (C) fails because Yeager's flight is not an instance of Crossfield's, and (D) because the 1947 flight could not be a result of the 1953 one.
cards.n: Sentence 2 comes second, so "subsequently" feels natural; check the dates and the verb tense, not the order of sentences.

cards.q:
"In 1665, Robert Hooke described the tiny compartments he saw in thin slices of cork, calling them cells. ______ in the 1670s, Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used microscopes of his own design to observe living single-celled organisms, which he called animalcules."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Subsequently,
(B) Previously,
(C) For instance,
(D) In other words,
cards.a: (A). The 1670s come after 1665, and sentence 2 describes a later step in early microscopy. (B) reverses the order. (C) fails because Leeuwenhoek's work is not an instance of Hooke's description, and (D) because sentence 2 is a new event, not a restatement.
cards.n: When both sentences carry dates, the dates decide; compare them before judging the relation by content.

cards.q:
"Emperor penguins breed during the Antarctic winter, incubating their eggs on sea ice in temperatures that can fall below −40°C. ______ Adélie penguins breed during the Antarctic spring and summer, nesting on ice-free rocky ground along the coast."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Nevertheless,
(B) For example,
(C) As a result,
(D) By contrast,
cards.a: (D). The text sets two species side by side and shows how they differ (winter on ice vs summer on rock), which is what by contrast (or in contrast) signals. (A) is the near-miss: nevertheless means "despite what was just said," and the Adélies' timing does not happen despite the emperors'. (C) and (B) make no sense between two separate species.
cards.h: → letter + comparison of two subjects vs despite
cards.n: Nevertheless and by contrast both "turn," but only by contrast compares two subjects; nevertheless needs one claim that the next sentence pushes against.

cards.q:
"The drug's effect varied sharply with the patients' age. ______ it lowered blood pressure substantially in patients under sixty but had no measurable effect in older patients."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) Specifically,
(B) Nevertheless,
(C) Similarly,
(D) In addition,
cards.a: (A). Sentence 2 spells out exactly how the effect varied with age, making the general claim precise, which is what specifically signals. (D) would need a separate, new point. (B) would need sentence 2 to push against sentence 1, and (C) would need a parallel case.
cards.h: → letter + general claim → the precise details
cards.n: Sentence 2 contains a contrast inside it ("but"), which tempts a contrast word; the transition relates sentence 2 to sentence 1, not its two halves.

cards.q:
"At its closest approach, the comet passes inside the orbit of Venus; at its farthest, it travels beyond the orbit of Neptune. ______ the comet's distance from the Sun changes enormously over the course of each orbit."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) However,
(B) For instance,
(C) In other words,
(D) In addition,
cards.a: (C). Sentence 2 restates sentence 1 in general terms: passing inside Venus's orbit and travelling beyond Neptune's IS an enormous change in distance. (B) runs the wrong way (the specific comes first, not after). (A) finds a contrast where there is none, and (D) treats a restatement as a new point.
cards.n: "For example" is the trap when the order is specific → general; an example follows the claim it illustrates.

cards.q:
"For decades, many economists assumed that raising the minimum wage would reduce employment among low-wage workers. A 1994 study comparing fast-food restaurants in New Jersey, which had raised its minimum wage, with those in neighboring Pennsylvania, which had not, found no such decline. ______ the study prompted a wave of new research into how employers actually respond to wage floors."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) However,
(B) For example,
(C) As a result,
(D) Nevertheless,
cards.a: (C). The blank links sentence 3 to sentence 2: the surprising finding prompted new research, a cause and its effect. (A) and (D) are tempting because the finding contradicted the assumption, but that contrast lies between sentences 1 and 2. Sentence 3 does not push against sentence 2. (B) fails because new research is not an instance of the study.
cards.h: → letter + which two sentences the blank joins
cards.n: The contrast has already happened by the blank; strong students carry it forward and pick "however."

cards.q:
"The sculptor Irena Vasko carved each of her early figures from a single block of stone, refusing to join separate pieces. ______ her later bronzes were each cast in a single pour rather than assembled from separately cast parts, as most large bronzes are."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) In contrast,
(B) Likewise,
(C) For example,
(D) Therefore,
cards.a: (B). The point of both sentences is the same principle: each work is made as one piece. The later bronzes follow the rule of the early stone figures, a similarity. (A) fixes on the surface difference (stone vs bronze, early vs late) rather than the relation the writer draws. (C) fails because the bronzes are not examples of stone carving, and (D) because the early practice does not cause the later one.
cards.h: → letter + what the writer says the two share
cards.n: Different materials and periods pull toward "in contrast"; the transition follows the writer's point, which is a shared principle.

cards.q:
"After the city added dedicated bus lanes on its busiest corridor, average commute times on the corridor's buses fell by eleven minutes. Ridership rose 18 percent, and complaints about late buses fell by half. ______ by every measure the city tracked, the pilot program succeeded."
Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
(A) For instance,
(B) In sum,
(C) Nevertheless,
(D) Meanwhile,
cards.a: (B). The last sentence draws together the results listed in the first two into one conclusion, which is what in sum (or in short, overall) signals. (A) would make the conclusion an example of the results, reversing their roles. (C) signals a concession, but nothing negative precedes it. (D) signals simultaneous events, and a conclusion is not an event.
cards.n: When sentence 3 generalizes, "for instance" is backward; examples come after a general claim, not before it.

cards.q: In a rhetorical synthesis question (notes, then "The student wants to... Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?"), what decides the answer, and in what order should you read?
cards.a: The goal decides it. Read the goal first and mark its exact words: emphasize a difference or a similarity, introduce to an audience unfamiliar with, present the aim and method, present the findings, explain an advantage, make a generalization. Every choice is accurate to the notes, so accuracy never separates them. Test each choice only against the goal, and require ALL of it: a difference names both things and how they differ; "unfamiliar" needs a description of who or what it is; "aim and method" needs both. Skim the notes only to confirm.
cards.h: → what decides + the reading order + the "all of it" test
cards.n: The most detailed or impressive choice is the usual trap; information that does not serve the goal is a reason to eliminate.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Benedita Varela is a Portuguese textile artist.
• She weaves large tapestries from fishing nets found on beaches near Porto.
• Her tapestry Maré (2019) is 12 meters long.
• Critics praise her for turning ocean debris into art.
The student wants to introduce Varela and her work to an audience unfamiliar with the artist. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Portuguese textile artist Benedita Varela weaves large tapestries from fishing nets found on beaches near Porto.
(B) Maré, a 2019 tapestry, is 12 meters long.
(C) Varela weaves tapestries such as Maré, which is 12 meters long.
(D) Critics praise Varela for turning ocean debris into art.
cards.a: (A). An unfamiliar audience must be told who she is (a Portuguese textile artist, full name) and what her work is (tapestries woven from discarded fishing nets). (B) describes one piece and never names her. (C) and (D) use "Varela" as if the reader already knew her, and (D) reports praise without saying what she makes.
cards.h: → letter + what an unfamiliar reader needs
cards.n: (D) sounds like the most important fact, but praise without identification leaves an unfamiliar reader asking "who?"

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• The kākāpō is a New Zealand parrot.
• It cannot fly and is active at night.
• The kea is a parrot of New Zealand's Southern Alps.
• It can fly and is active mainly during the day.
• Both species are endangered.
The student wants to emphasize a difference between the two parrots. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) The kākāpō and the kea are both endangered New Zealand parrots.
(B) The kākāpō is a flightless New Zealand parrot that is active at night.
(C) The kea, a parrot of New Zealand's Southern Alps, is active mainly during the day.
(D) The kākāpō cannot fly and is active at night, whereas the kea can fly and is active mainly by day.
cards.a: (D). A difference needs both birds and a contrast between them: flightless and nocturnal vs flying and active by day, joined by "whereas." (A) states a similarity. (C) and (B) each describe only one bird, so nothing is contrasted.
cards.n: (B) contains the most striking fact (a parrot that cannot fly), but a difference needs the second term; one bird alone emphasizes nothing.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• The Hubble Space Telescope (launched 1990) orbits Earth about 500 kilometers up.
• Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
• The James Webb Space Telescope (launched 2021) operates about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth.
• Webb observes mainly infrared light.
The student wants to emphasize a difference in where the two telescopes operate. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Hubble orbits about 500 kilometers above Earth, while Webb operates about 1.5 million kilometers away.
(B) Hubble and Webb are both space telescopes.
(C) Webb observes mainly infrared light, while Hubble observes mainly visible and ultraviolet light.
(D) Hubble was launched in 1990, more than three decades before Webb.
cards.a: (A). The goal asks for a difference in WHERE they operate, and only (A) contrasts their locations. (C) is a real difference, but in the light they observe, not where they are. (D) contrasts launch dates. (B) states a similarity.
cards.h: → letter + which difference the goal names
cards.n: (C) is a well-formed contrast of both telescopes, so it survives a quick check; the goal's word "where" rules it out.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Hydrologist Nadia Ferreira's team studied beaver dams.
• They wanted to learn whether the dams raise groundwater levels during droughts.
• For three years, they measured groundwater in 40 wells, 20 near dams and 20 far from them.
• In drought months, groundwater near dams was about 0.5 meters higher.
The student wants to present the study's aim and methodology. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Ferreira's team found that in drought months, groundwater near dams was about 0.5 meters higher.
(B) To learn whether beaver dams raise groundwater during droughts, Ferreira's team monitored 40 wells, half near dams, for three years.
(C) Ferreira is a hydrologist whose team studied beaver dams.
(D) Beaver dams may raise groundwater levels during droughts, a question Ferreira's team studied.
cards.a: (B). It gives the aim ("to learn whether...") and the method (three years of measurements in 40 wells, half near dams). (A) gives the result, which is neither aim nor method. (C) gives only who studied what. (D) gives roughly the aim but no method.
cards.n: (A) is the most interesting sentence, and results are what a summary usually reports; the goal names aim and method, and results are neither.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• The axolotl is a salamander that can regrow lost limbs.
• Biologist Rafael Ortega's team studied how axolotls regrow limbs.
• They found that a protein they named Rg-7 is needed for regrowth to begin.
• Axolotls lacking Rg-7 healed their wounds but did not regrow limbs.
The student wants to present the study's finding to an audience unfamiliar with axolotls. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Ortega's team found that axolotls lacking the protein Rg-7 healed their wounds but did not regrow limbs.
(B) The axolotl is a salamander that can regrow lost limbs.
(C) Ortega's team studied how the axolotl regrows its limbs.
(D) Ortega's team found that the axolotl, a salamander that can regrow lost limbs, needs a protein called Rg-7 for regrowth to begin.
cards.a: (D). The goal has two parts: the finding (Rg-7 is needed for regrowth to begin) and enough description for a reader who does not know what an axolotl is (a salamander that can regrow limbs). (A) gives a finding but never says what an axolotl is. (B) describes the animal but gives no finding. (C) gives neither.
cards.h: → letter + both parts of the goal
cards.n: Two-part goals are where 730s lose points: (A) and (B) each do one part perfectly, so each feels complete.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Octavia E. Butler (1947–2006) was an American science fiction writer.
• In 1995, she became the first science fiction writer to win a MacArthur Fellowship.
• Her 1979 novel Kindred follows Dana, a Black writer in 1976 California.
• Dana is repeatedly pulled back in time to a plantation in antebellum Maryland.
The student wants to introduce Kindred to an audience already familiar with Butler. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Butler was the first science fiction writer to win a MacArthur Fellowship.
(B) Octavia E. Butler (1947–2006) wrote Kindred.
(C) In Butler's Kindred (1979), Dana, a Black writer in 1976 California, is repeatedly pulled back in time to a plantation in antebellum Maryland.
(D) Butler won a MacArthur Fellowship in 1995, sixteen years after Kindred appeared.
cards.a: (C). The thing to introduce is the novel, and the audience already knows Butler, so the sentence should give Kindred's premise and can say "Butler" without explanation. (A) and (D) are about Butler, which this audience does not need. (B) names the novel but says nothing about it.
cards.h: → letter + what the audience already knows
cards.n: (A) introduces someone, which feels like "introducing"; the goal names the novel as the thing to introduce and says the author needs no introduction.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Many plants in dry regions store water in thick tissues.
• The saguaro cactus stores water in its pleated stem, which expands after rain.
• The baobab tree stores water in its massive trunk.
• Aloe vera stores water in its fleshy leaves.
The student wants to make a generalization about how plants in dry regions store water. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Many plants in dry regions store water in thick tissues, whether in stems, like the saguaro, in trunks, like the baobab, or in leaves, like aloe vera.
(B) The saguaro cactus stores water in its pleated stem, which expands after rain.
(C) The baobab tree stores water in its trunk, while aloe vera stores water in its leaves.
(D) Aloe vera stores water in its fleshy leaves.
cards.a: (A). A generalization makes a claim about plants in dry regions as a group, and (A) does so (the examples only support it). (B) and (D) are single cases, and (C) sets two cases side by side without stating what they have in common.
cards.n: (C) mentions two plants, which can feel general; two examples are still examples until a sentence states the pattern.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Engineer Lucía Ferrand developed a concrete mix that replaces 40 percent of the cement with ground glass.
• Producing it releases about 35 percent less carbon dioxide than producing standard concrete.
• In tests, it was as strong as standard concrete.
• It costs about 8 percent more to produce.
The student wants to explain an advantage of Ferrand's mix over standard concrete. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Ferrand's mix costs about 8 percent more to produce than standard concrete.
(B) Ferrand is an engineer who developed a new concrete mix.
(C) In tests, Ferrand's mix was as strong as standard concrete.
(D) Producing Ferrand's mix releases about 35 percent less carbon dioxide than producing standard concrete.
cards.a: (D). An advantage is a way the mix is better than standard concrete, and (D) gives one: about 35 percent less carbon dioxide. (A) gives a disadvantage. (C) shows the mix is equal in strength, not better. (B) introduces the engineer without comparing anything.
cards.n: (C) sounds positive, but "as strong as" is parity; an advantage requires the new thing to be better on some measure.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Arctic terns breed in the Arctic and spend the northern winter in Antarctic waters.
• A 2010 tracking study found that the terns it followed flew about 70,900 kilometers a year on average.
• Arctic terns can live more than 30 years.
• An adult weighs about 100 grams.
The student wants to emphasize how far an Arctic tern may travel over its lifetime. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
(A) Flying about 70,900 kilometers a year and living more than 30 years, an Arctic tern may cover an enormous distance in its lifetime.
(B) An Arctic tern weighs only about 100 grams yet flies about 70,900 kilometers a year.
(C) Arctic terns breed in the Arctic and spend the northern winter in Antarctic waters.
(D) A 2010 tracking study measured how far Arctic terns fly each year.
cards.a: (A). A lifetime distance needs both the yearly distance and the lifespan, and only (A) combines them. (B) gives a striking yearly figure, but a year is not a lifetime. (C) describes the route without a distance, and (D) says a distance was measured without giving it.
cards.h: → letter + which two facts the goal needs
cards.n: (B) has the big number and a vivid contrast (tiny bird, huge distance); the goal word "lifetime" requires the lifespan too.

cards.q:
A student has taken these notes:
• Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa (about 1831) is a woodblock print.
• It shows a huge wave about to crash over three boats.
• Hiroshige's Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake (1857) is also a woodblock print.
• It shows people crossing a bridge in a rainstorm.
• Both artists worked in the Japanese ukiyo-e tradition.
The student wants to emphasize a similarity between the two prints. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
